LiteLLM admin-route request with suspicious / mismatched Host header (CVE-2026-49468) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the actual exploit primitive — a request to a protected LiteLLM management endpoint (/key/*, /user/*, /team/*, /model/*, /customer/*, /spend/*, /organization/*) where the Host header looks crafted: an IP literal, contains `;` / `@` / `..`, has a path component, or differs from the load-balancer's known SNI/server_name. Targets the request shape called out in the GHSA: Starlette reconstructs `request.url.path` from Host, so the auth gate sees a different route than FastAPI dispatches. Rationale: The GHSA explicitly attributes the bypass to Starlette rebuilding `request.url.path` from the Host header, so anomalous Host values on the seven documented management-route prefixes are the highest-signal request-layer indicator of CVE-2026-49468 exploitation. Specific prefixes cross-checked against the LiteLLM management-endpoints docs. Cross-checked against: • https://deepwiki.com/BerriAI/litellm/3.5-management-endpoints-and-multi-tenancy • https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/proxy/public_routes • https://badhost.org/
ATT&CKT1190 T1036
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal Kubernetes probes hitting the pod IP directly with `Host: <pod-ip>:4000`
  • Load-balancer/CDN health checks that strip or omit the Host header
  • Pen-test or vuln-scan tooling that intentionally fuzzes Host
  • Misconfigured client that sends `Host: localhost` to a public ingress
Suppression filter
| where not (SrcIp startswith "10." or SrcIp startswith "172.16." or SrcIp startswith "192.168.") and HostHdr !startswith "localhost"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request — confirm the Host value is genuinely anomalous (not just an internal probe) and check the response code; a 200/201 with a path-traversal Host is the smoking gun. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF, rotate any LiteLLM master keys / virtual keys that could have been issued or read, and confirm the proxy is upgraded to ≥1.84.0 or fronted by a Host-validating reverse proxy. 3) Hunt: chain to UC3 (401→200 from the same SrcIp), UC4 (route enumeration), and UC5 (unauthenticated admin success) across the prior 30 days.
let LiteLLMAdminPaths = dynamic(["/key/","/user/","/team/","/model/","/customer/","/spend/","/organization/"]);
let KnownGoodHosts = dynamic(["litellm.internal","ai-gw.corp"]);
(union isfuzzy=true
  (W3CIISLog
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
   | where csUriStem has_any (LiteLLMAdminPaths)
   | extend HostHdr = tostring(csHost), SrcIp = tostring(cIP), Path = tostring(csUriStem), Method = tostring(csMethod), Status = toint(scStatus)),
  (CommonSecurityLog
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
   | where DeviceProduct has_any ("NGINX","Apache","ALB","AzureFrontDoor","AzureWAF","CloudFront")
   | where RequestURL has_any (LiteLLMAdminPaths)
   | extend HostHdr = tostring(DestinationHostName), SrcIp = tostring(SourceIP), Path = tostring(RequestURL), Method = tostring(RequestMethod), Status = toint(EventOutcome)))
| extend HostAnomaly = case(
    HostHdr matches regex @"^\d{1,3}(\.\d{1,3}){3}(:\d+)?$", "ip_literal",
    HostHdr matches regex @"[;@]", "injection_char",
    HostHdr contains "..", "path_traversal",
    HostHdr contains "/", "path_in_host",
    isempty(HostHdr), "empty_host",
    not(HostHdr in~ (KnownGoodHosts)) and HostHdr !endswith ".corp" and HostHdr !endswith ".internal", "unexpected_host",
    "normal")
| where HostAnomaly != "normal"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIp, HostHdr, Path, Method, Status, HostAnomaly
| summarize Count=count(), Paths=make_set(Path,10), Statuses=make_set(Status,10), Anomalies=make_set(HostAnomaly,5) by SrcIp, HostHdr, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: LiteLLM Admin Route Hit with Anomalous Host Header (CVE-2026-49468)
id: 7e3a4d2c-9f1b-4c8e-8a72-1d2b3c4e5f60
status: experimental
description: A request to a LiteLLM management route (/key, /user, /team, /model, /customer, /spend, /organization) carries a Host header that is an IP literal, contains injection characters, has a path component, or is empty — indicative of CVE-2026-49468 exploitation attempts.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4xpc-pv4p-pm3w
  - https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/releases/tag/v1.84.0
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/17
tags:
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.t1036
  - attack.defense_evasion
logsource:
  category: webserver
detection:
  selection_path:
    cs-uri-stem|startswith:
      - '/key/'
      - '/user/'
      - '/team/'
      - '/model/'
      - '/customer/'
      - '/spend/'
      - '/organization/'
  host_anomaly:
    cs-host|re: '^(\d{1,3}\.){3}\d{1,3}(:\d+)?$|[;@]|\.\./|/'
  condition: selection_path and host_anomaly
falsepositives:
  - Internal monitoring probes that legitimately hit the proxy by IP address
  - Load balancer health checks that omit the Host header
level: high
(source:nginx OR source:apache OR source:aws.alb OR source:azure.frontdoor) (@http.url_details.path:(\/key\/* OR \/user\/* OR \/team\/* OR \/model\/* OR \/customer\/* OR \/spend\/* OR \/organization\/*)) AND (@http.url_details.host:/^[0-9]{1,3}\.[0-9]{1,3}\.[0-9]{1,3}\.[0-9]{1,3}(:[0-9]+)?$/ OR @http.url_details.host:*\;* OR @http.url_details.host:*\@* OR @http.url_details.host:*\/* OR @http.url_details.host:*\.\.*)
# log group: /aws/applicationelb/<litellm-alb>
fields @timestamp, client_ip, request_url, target_status_code, domain_name, request_verb, user_agent
| filter request_url like /\/(key|user|team|model|customer|spend|organization)\//
| filter (domain_name like /^[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+/ or domain_name like /[;@]/ or domain_name like /\.\./ or domain_name like /\// or domain_name = "-")
| sort @timestamp desc
| limit 200

| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(Web.http_method) as methods, values(Web.status) as statuses, values(Web.url) as urls, values(Web.dest) as dests from datamodel=Web where (Web.uri_path="/key/*" OR Web.uri_path="/user/*" OR Web.uri_path="/team/*" OR Web.uri_path="/model/*" OR Web.uri_path="/customer/*" OR Web.uri_path="/spend/*" OR Web.uri_path="/organization/*") by Web.src, Web.dest, host, _time span=5m | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | join type=left host [search index=* sourcetype IN ("nginx:plus:kv","nginx:plus:access","access_combined","ms:iis:auto","aws:elasticloadbalancing:accesslogs") (uri_path="/key/*" OR uri_path="/user/*" OR uri_path="/team/*" OR uri_path="/model/*" OR uri_path="/customer/*" OR uri_path="/spend/*" OR uri_path="/organization/*") | rex field=_raw "(?i)host:\s*(?<host_hdr>[^\s;]+)" | eval host_anomaly=case(match(host_hdr,"(?i)^\d{1,3}(\.\d{1,3}){3}"),"ip_literal", match(host_hdr,"[;@]"),"injection_char", match(host_hdr,"\.\."),"path_traversal", match(host_hdr,"/"),"path_in_host", isnull(host_hdr) OR host_hdr="","empty_host", 1==1,"normal") | where host_anomaly!="normal" | stats values(host_hdr) as host_headers, values(host_anomaly) as anomalies by host] | where isnotnull(anomalies)
LiteLLM admin endpoint 401→200 sequence from same source (auth bypass) AIExploitation Medium
Looks for the post-exploitation signature of CVE-2026-49468: the same client IP receives 401/403 on a LiteLLM management route, then within five minutes lands a 200/201 on the same or a sibling admin route. A clean bypass typically shows the failure→success transition because the attacker probes for valid Host crafting before it lands. Rationale: The article describes 'unauthenticated access to protected management routes' — operationally an attacker probes, gets 401/403, mutates Host, then lands a 200. The 401→200 transition on the documented management-route prefixes is the cleanest post-exploit pattern, particularly when the Host header differs between the failed and successful request. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4xpc-pv4p-pm3w • https://deepwiki.com/BerriAI/litellm/3.5-management-endpoints-and-multi-tenancy
ATT&CKT1190 T1078
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A user typos / forgets their API key, retries with the right one — same SrcIp, 401 then 200
  • Token rotation: client briefly uses an expired key (401) then refreshed key (200)
  • CI/CD pipeline tests that intentionally probe with no token to assert 401, then run authenticated tests
  • Load-balancer reissuing a session after a brief auth-cache miss
Suppression filter
| where HostHeaderDivergence == "yes" or SuccessCount > FailCount * 0.5
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the raw requests for the SrcIp inside the 5-min window. Compare the Authorization header / api-key cookie between the 401 and the 200 — if they're identical (or both empty) and only the Host differs, that is exploitation. 2) Contain: revoke any keys the successful request returned/created (GET /key/info, POST /key/generate), block the SrcIp at the WAF, and confirm the proxy is on ≥1.84.0 or behind a Host-validating front door. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC4 to see if the same SrcIp went on to enumerate further admin categories, and check for new /key/generate or /user/new calls in the prior 24h.
let LiteLLMAdminPaths = dynamic(["/key/","/user/","/team/","/model/","/customer/","/spend/","/organization/"]);
let Window = 5m;
let AdminHits =
  (union isfuzzy=true
    (W3CIISLog | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d) | where csUriStem has_any (LiteLLMAdminPaths) | project TimeGenerated, SrcIp=cIP, Path=csUriStem, Status=toint(scStatus), Host=csHost),
    (CommonSecurityLog | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d) | where RequestURL has_any (LiteLLMAdminPaths) | project TimeGenerated, SrcIp=SourceIP, Path=RequestURL, Status=toint(EventOutcome), Host=DestinationHostName))
  | where Status in (401,403,200,201,204);
AdminHits
| summarize FailCount=countif(Status in (401,403)),
            SuccessCount=countif(Status in (200,201,204)),
            FailPaths=make_set_if(Path, Status in (401,403), 10),
            SuccessPaths=make_set_if(Path, Status in (200,201,204), 10),
            FailHosts=make_set_if(Host, Status in (401,403), 5),
            SuccessHosts=make_set_if(Host, Status in (200,201,204), 5),
            FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated)
            by SrcIp, bin(TimeGenerated, Window)
| where FailCount >= 1 and SuccessCount >= 1
| extend HostHeaderDivergence = iif(tostring(FailHosts) != tostring(SuccessHosts), "yes", "no")
| order by HostHeaderDivergence desc, LastSeen desc
(source:nginx OR source:apache OR source:aws.alb OR source:azure.frontdoor) @http.url_details.path:(\/key\/* OR \/user\/* OR \/team\/* OR \/model\/* OR \/customer\/* OR \/spend\/* OR \/organization\/*) @http.status_code:(401 OR 403 OR 200 OR 201 OR 204)
# log group: /aws/applicationelb/<litellm-alb>
fields @timestamp, client_ip, request_url, target_status_code, domain_name
| filter request_url like /\/(key|user|team|model|customer|spend|organization)\//
| filter target_status_code in [401, 403, 200, 201, 204]
| stats count(*) as hits, sum(if(target_status_code in [401,403], 1, 0)) as failures, sum(if(target_status_code in [200,201,204], 1, 0)) as successes, earliest(@timestamp) as first_seen, latest(@timestamp) as last_seen, count_distinct(domain_name) as host_hdrs by client_ip, bin(5m)
| filter failures >= 1 and successes >= 1
| sort last_seen desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count, values(Web.uri_path) as paths, values(Web.status) as statuses, min(_time) as firstSeen, max(_time) as lastSeen from datamodel=Web where (Web.uri_path="/key/*" OR Web.uri_path="/user/*" OR Web.uri_path="/team/*" OR Web.uri_path="/model/*" OR Web.uri_path="/customer/*" OR Web.uri_path="/spend/*" OR Web.uri_path="/organization/*") by Web.src, Web.dest, _time span=5m | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | eval failed=if(match(mvjoin(statuses,","), "401|403"),1,0), succeeded=if(match(mvjoin(statuses,","),"200|201|204"),1,0) | where failed=1 AND succeeded=1 AND mvcount(paths)>=2 | convert ctime(firstSeen) ctime(lastSeen)
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(Web.uri_path) as paths, values(Web.status) as statuses, min(_time) as firstSeen, max(_time) as lastSeen from datamodel=Web where (Web.uri_path="/key/*" OR Web.uri_path="/user/*" OR Web.uri_path="/team/*" OR Web.uri_path="/model/*" OR Web.uri_path="/customer/*" OR Web.uri_path="/spend/*" OR Web.uri_path="/organization/*") by Web.src, Web.dest, _time span=5m | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | eval failed=if(match(mvjoin(statuses,","), "401|403"),1,0), succeeded=if(match(mvjoin(statuses,","),"200|201|204"),1,0) | where failed=1 AND succeeded=1 AND mvcount(paths)>=2 | convert ctime(firstSeen) ctime(lastSeen)
LiteLLM rapid admin-route enumeration across distinct management categories AIActions on Objectives Medium
Flags a single source IP making successful (2xx) requests to three or more distinct LiteLLM management-route categories within 10 minutes — e.g. /key + /user + /team + /spend. Post-bypass an attacker fans out across the documented management endpoints to inventory keys, users and budgets; legitimate operators typically work in one category at a time. Rationale: LiteLLM management endpoints are split into seven documented category prefixes (key/user/team/model/customer/spend/organization per the management-endpoints docs). A single SrcIp touching three or more in a 10-min window is the canonical post-bypass fan-out shape and is far above legitimate-admin baseline (admins usually work one category at a time via the UI). Cross-checked against: • https://deepwiki.com/BerriAI/litellm/3.5-management-endpoints-and-multi-tenancy • https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/proxy/virtual_keys
ATT&CKT1046 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • LiteLLM Admin UI bulk operations (e.g. an admin onboarding a new team triggers /team/new + /user/new + /key/generate + /spend/* in quick succession)
  • Terraform / Pulumi runs against the LiteLLM provider that touch many resource categories from a single CI runner IP
  • Backup/export jobs that GET /key/list, /user/list, /team/list nightly
  • Migration scripts run by SRE after an upgrade
Suppression filter
| where SrcIp !in (dynamic(["<admin-jumpbox-ip>","<ci-runner-ip>"]))
Response runbook
1) Triage: check whether SrcIp is a known admin/CI source (jump host, GH Actions runner). Pull the User-Agent string — legitimate admins use browsers; attack tooling is typically python-requests, curl, or empty. 2) Contain: if SrcIp is unknown/external, block at WAF and rotate every key returned from /key/list/info during the window. 3) Hunt: enumerate /key/generate, /user/new, /team/new calls in the prior 24h to find any persistence artefacts the attacker created; also pivot to UC2/UC3 on the same SrcIp.

Unauthenticated success on LiteLLM admin endpoint (Authorization header absent) AIExploitation High
Direct expression of the GHSA: a 200/201/204 response to a /key, /user, /team, /model, /customer, /spend or /organization endpoint where the request carried no Authorization header AND no `api_key`/`x-api-key`/`x-litellm-key` parameter. Pre-1.84.0 this should be impossible for protected routes; a hit is high-confidence exploitation of CVE-2026-49468. Rationale: GHSA wording is precise: 'allow unauthenticated access to protected management routes.' A successful 2xx on the seven documented admin prefixes with no auth artefact present is the exploit definition, not a heuristic. Lowest plausible FP rate of the request-layer detections. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4xpc-pv4p-pm3w • https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/proxy/public_routes
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Proxy layer in front of LiteLLM strips Authorization before forwarding-and-logging (look at the inner-proxy logs instead)
  • Health-check endpoints accidentally aliased under /key/health by a custom deployment
  • Internal mTLS-terminated traffic where auth happens at the cert layer and no Authorization header is sent
  • Service-to-service calls using IP-allowlist instead of bearer auth (rare in LiteLLM deployments)
Suppression filter
| where CsHost !startswith "localhost" and CIp !startswith "10." and CIp !startswith "127."
Response runbook
1) Triage: re-pull the raw access log entry — confirm the Authorization header is genuinely absent (not just truncated by log shaping) and that the response body returned real data (not an error page with a 200 status). 2) Contain: rotate every LiteLLM master key and virtual key issued in the last 30 days, force-upgrade the proxy to ≥1.84.0, and front the listener with a `server_name` allowlist immediately. 3) Hunt: enumerate /key/generate calls the SrcIp made (new attacker-owned keys), audit /user/new for backdoor accounts, and check outbound LLM-provider calls in the next 24h for cost-abuse / data-exfil via newly minted keys.

LiteLLM proxy reconnaissance — /health /version /docs probes on default ports AIReconnaissance Medium
Detects pre-exploitation discovery of internet-exposed LiteLLM instances: requests to /health, /version, /docs, /openapi.json, /sso/key/generate or the Swagger UI on LiteLLM's default listener ports (4000, 8000, 8001) from external/non-internal sources, especially when paired with scanner-style user agents. Rationale: LiteLLM ships with documented public introspection routes (/health/liveliness, /health/readiness, /version, /docs, /openapi.json, /redoc) and runs on port 4000 by default — these are the natural pre-exploit fingerprinting targets before an attacker tries CVE-2026-49468. Default-port + path-set combination keeps the detection LiteLLM-specific rather than generic web scanning. Cross-checked against: • https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/proxy/public_routes • https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/
ATT&CKT1046 T1595.002
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • External uptime monitors (Pingdom, UptimeRobot, Datadog Synthetics) hitting /health repeatedly
  • Cloud provider load-balancer health probes from public LB IPs
  • Legitimate internal tooling using python-requests/curl from a misclassified subnet
  • Security team's own external attack-surface scanner (Detectify, Tenable.io) hitting /docs and /openapi.json
Suppression filter
| where SrcIp !in (dynamic(["<uptime-monitor-ip-1>","<uptime-monitor-ip-2>"])) and UA !contains "Pingdom" and UA !contains "UptimeRobot" and UA !contains "DatadogSynthetics"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm SrcIp is genuinely external and not a known uptime monitor or LB probe IP; check if /docs/openapi.json was hit (signals an attacker reading the API surface, not a health probe). 2) Contain: if external + scanner UA, block at WAF and place the listener behind an authenticated CDN/WAF that validates Host. Treat as precursor to UC2/UC5 — actively look for follow-on /key /user /team requests from the same SrcIp. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC2 (Host header anomalies), UC3 (401→200), UC4 (admin enumeration) on the same SrcIp in the prior 7 days; if confirmed exploitation likely, escalate to IR and rotate keys.

Malicious JetBrains Marketplace plugin install by ID (Aikido campaign) AIInstallation High
Hunts for installation of the 15 known-malicious JetBrains Marketplace plugin JARs / extracted plugin directories on developer workstations. File path + plugin ID is the highest-fidelity pivot because the plugin IDs are unique campaign artefacts. Rationale: Anchored on the 15 plugin IDs explicitly named in the Aikido report and confirmed by BleepingComputer's independent analysis of ord.cp.code.ai.kit. Plugin IDs are unique campaign artefacts so false positives are essentially nil. Cross-checked with the BleepingComputer article body listing all IDs. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/malicious-jetbrains-marketplace-plugins-steal-ai-api-keys-from-developers/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate JetBrains plugin updates that happen to share a similar naming convention (very unlikely given the exact IDs)
  • Security researcher / IR team intentionally pulling the samples into a lab
  • Plugin ID collision in a legitimate marketplace package (no such collision observed)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the host, the developer account, and which plugin ID dropped. Cross-reference with DeviceProcessEvents for the JetBrains IDE process that wrote the file. 2) Contain: isolate the workstation in Defender; instruct the developer to immediately rotate any OpenAI, DeepSeek, SiliconFlow, and other AI provider API keys saved in IDE settings; uninstall the plugin from the JetBrains Marketplace and disable plugin auto-install for the user group. 3) Hunt: pivot on developer account to find other workstations with the same plugin; query SaaS provider billing/usage logs for the rotated AI keys to detect attacker abuse before rotation.

JetBrains IDE outbound to attacker C2 39.107.60.51 over plaintext HTTP AICommand & Control High
Alerting detection for the campaign's hardcoded C2/exfil endpoint. Matches any outbound network connection from a JetBrains IDE process to 39.107.60.51 — this is where both the stolen API keys leave and the resold keys arrive. Rationale: 39.107.60.51 is the hardcoded C2/exfil endpoint named in the Aikido report and reproduced verbatim in the BleepingComputer article. Process scope to JetBrains IDE binaries (and bundled javaw.exe which executes plugin JARs) makes this near-zero-FP. We also keep the bare ImNetworkSession filter for Sentinel so the IP hit fires regardless of which sensor reported it. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/malicious-jetbrains-marketplace-plugins-steal-ai-api-keys-from-developers/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat researcher detonating the plugin in an analysis VM connected to the corporate proxy
  • Reverse-engineer fetching the C2 host for IOC enrichment
  • Customer-support agent reproducing the issue on a developer's machine
  • Sinkholed / takedown traffic if the IP is later seized
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the JetBrains IDE process, plugin directory contents, and the developer account. Pull the AdditionalFields from the network event to confirm the URI path /api/software/key. 2) Contain: isolate the host, force-rotate every AI provider API key the developer has stored in JetBrains settings (OpenAI, DeepSeek, SiliconFlow, Anthropic, etc.); add 39.107.60.51 to perimeter blocklist. 3) Hunt: sweep DeviceNetworkEvents and proxy logs across the org for any other host that has contacted 39.107.60.51 — even non-developer machines if the proxy is shared.

Outbound HTTP request to URI path /api/software/key (plugin exfil endpoint) AIActions on Objectives High
URI-based detection for the campaign's exfil path. The path /api/software/key is the literal endpoint the plugins POST stolen AI API keys to. Catches variants of the campaign that may rotate IP/host but keep the URI. Rationale: Path /api/software/key is the literal exfil URI named in the article and quoted in the IOC list — short, vendor-specific, and not a path any legitimate AI provider serves. Catches the campaign even if attackers move off 39.107.60.51 to a new front. Cross-checked with the original Aikido write-up referenced by BleepingComputer. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/malicious-jetbrains-marketplace-plugins-steal-ai-api-keys-from-developers/
ATT&CKT1041 T1567
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal product that happens to expose an unrelated /api/software/key endpoint (rare — exclude known internal hostnames)
  • Security tooling replaying captured PCAPs of the campaign for IR practice
  • License-key servers in pre-existing third-party software (exclude known good hosts)
Suppression filter
| where not (DestinationHostName endswith ".corp.local" or RequestURL startswith "https://internal-licensing.")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the request body if proxy logs include it; confirm the IDE process initiated the call. Cross-check the destination IP — current campaign uses 39.107.60.51 but the URI may stay constant across IP rotations. 2) Contain: rotate all AI provider API keys the affected developer has stored in JetBrains; block the destination IP and URI pattern at the perimeter; quarantine the plugin directory. 3) Hunt: search proxy logs for the same URI from any other host in the previous 30 days; check whether the destination uses a different IP in earlier hits (campaign infra rotation).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "/api/software/key" or AdditionalFields has "/api/software/key"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, AdditionalFields
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
  (ImWebSession

    | where Url has "/api/software/key" or UrlOriginal has "/api/software/key"
    | project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, HttpMethod, Url, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent),
  (CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where RequestURL has "/api/software/key"
    | project TimeGenerated, SourceHostName=SourceHostName, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

JetBrains IDE plaintext HTTP to bare-IP destination (no domain) — plugin exfil shape AICommand & Control Medium
Hunting query for the broader campaign-shape: any JetBrains IDE process making plaintext HTTP (port 80) calls directly to a bare IPv4 (no DNS resolution / no Host header domain). Legitimate JetBrains products always talk to *.jetbrains.com / *.openai.com / etc over HTTPS, so this shape is anomalous. Rationale: JetBrains IDEs talk to known cloud endpoints (jetbrains.com, plugins.jetbrains.com, openai.com, anthropic.com, deepseek.com, etc.) over HTTPS. Plaintext HTTP to a bare IPv4 with no host-header domain is the campaign's signature — confirmed by the 39.107.60.51 IP and HTTP scheme in both the Aikido report and the BleepingComputer reproduction. Hunting tier because new dev environments and self-hosted Maven/JFrog mirrors can trip this — see FP filters. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/malicious-jetbrains-marketplace-plugins-steal-ai-api-keys-from-developers/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1095
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Self-hosted Maven / JFrog Artifactory / npm proxy reached by IP rather than DNS
  • Internal CI/CD container registry on a private network IP exposed via NAT
  • Developer testing a local microservice from inside the IDE's HTTP Client tool
  • Legacy on-prem package mirror that hasn't been migrated to TLS
  • Pre-installed JetBrains license server reached by IP
Suppression filter
| where DstIpAddr !in ("<artifactory-ip>","<jfrog-ip>","<internal-pypi-ip>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: list distinct destination IPs per developer host; for each unknown IP, WHOIS + passive DNS to determine if it's a corporate asset. Pull plugin directory contents on top hits. 2) Contain: where the IP matches the Aikido IOC list (or any other suspect Chinese-net-block IP), rotate that developer's AI provider keys and isolate the workstation; for unknown destinations, add to monitoring before blocking. 3) Hunt: pivot the destination IP across all sources for 30 days; check JetBrains plugin install events from the host in the same window; look for cluster of developer hosts sharing the same suspicious destination.

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Install of TeamPCP Miasma/Hades-compromised npm or PyPI package versions
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Post-install node or python child process beaconing to non-registry public destination
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Package-manager install descendant reads .npmrc / pip.conf credentials
Install of TeamPCP Miasma/Hades-compromised npm or PyPI package versions AIDelivery High
Hunts file-system evidence of the specific compromised package@version pairs (ensmallen 0.8.101, mflux-streamlit 0.0.3/0.0.4, embiggen 0.11.97, gpsea 0.9.14, pyphetools 0.9.120, nhmpy 2.4.7, ppkt2synergy 0.1.1) being unpacked into node_modules or site-packages on developer endpoints. Article-specific because it pivots on the named IOCs from the June 3/8 2026 campaign, not on a generic package-install template. Rationale: Uses the exact IOC package names from the kill-chain block (Miasma npm wave June 3 / Hades PyPI wave June 8 2026). Anchoring on node_modules/site-packages path plus the named packages avoids false positives from generic file-create noise. Cross-checked StepSecurity blog and MITRE T1195.002. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/prevent-npm-and-python-supply-chain-attacks-on-developer-machines-with-package-configs • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/002/
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher intentionally fetching IOC samples for analysis
  • Internal mirror legitimately serving an old, clean version of the package name reused after maintainer recovery
  • Air-gapped reproduction lab unpacking previously archived tarballs
  • CI runner reproducing a historical lockfile resolution for incident-response purposes
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("7z.exe","WinRAR.exe","tar.exe") and FolderPath !contains @"\IR-Samples\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the package@version on disk matches an IOC version; pull package.json/PKG-INFO and the resolved-from URL (npm cache / pip wheel cache). 2) Contain: isolate the endpoint, revoke all npm and PyPI tokens accessible from that user (~/.npmrc, ~/.pypirc, keyring), force-rotate any cloud SSO refresh tokens, and block the IOC versions at the internal Artifactory/Nexus mirror. 3) Hunt: search the fleet for other endpoints that resolved the same registry hosts in the last 14 days, audit npm/PyPI publish events under that user's tokens for republished tarballs, and verify no downstream repos have lockfiles pinning the bad versions.
let pkgs = dynamic(["ensmallen","mflux-streamlit","embiggen","gpsea","pyphetools","nhmpy","ppkt2synergy"]);
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\node_modules\", "/site-packages/")
| where FileName =~ "package.json" or FileName endswith ".dist-info" or FileName =~ "PKG-INFO" or FileName =~ "METADATA"
| where FolderPath has_any (pkgs)
| extend MatchedPkg = tostring(pkgs[array_index_of(pkgs, extract(@"(?i)(?:node_modules[\\/]|site-packages[\\/])([a-z0-9_\-]+)", 1, FolderPath))])
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName, MatchedPkg
| order by Timestamp desc
let pkgs = dynamic(["ensmallen","mflux-streamlit","embiggen","gpsea","pyphetools","nhmpy","ppkt2synergy"]);
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\node_modules\", "/site-packages/")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("package.json","PKG-INFO","METADATA") or TargetFilePath endswith ".dist-info"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (pkgs)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
title: Miasma/Hades Compromised Package Install

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_path="*\\node_modules\\ensmallen\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\node_modules\\mflux-streamlit\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\node_modules\\embiggen\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\node_modules\\gpsea\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\node_modules\\pyphetools\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\node_modules\\nhmpy\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\node_modules\\ppkt2synergy\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/site-packages/ensmallen*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/site-packages/embiggen*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/site-packages/gpsea*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/site-packages/pyphetools*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)

Package-manager install descendant reads .npmrc / pip.conf credentials AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects credential-bearing config reads (.npmrc, .yarnrc, .yarnrc.yml, bunfig.toml, .pypirc, pip.conf) by short-lived processes whose ancestor is npm/pnpm/yarn/bun/pip — the exact harvest behaviour Miasma/Hades use to steal publishing tokens. Article-specific because the file set and parent-process set are taken directly from the campaign write-up. Rationale: Article explicitly names the credential files harvested by Miasma/Hades ("a static token sitting in a .npmrc is not just a hygiene issue, it is the fuel these worms run on"). Pairing the named files with package-manager ancestors gives strong intent signal without flagging routine editor opens. Cross-checked StepSecurity write-up and MITRE T1552.001. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/prevent-npm-and-python-supply-chain-attacks-on-developer-machines-with-package-configs • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/001/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1528
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer running `npm whoami` or `pip config list` which legitimately reads the same config files
  • IDE language-server (VS Code Python/Node extensions) parsing the user's config on workspace open
  • CI bootstrap step that reads .npmrc to set up authenticated proxy
  • Secrets-scanning agent (gitleaks, trufflehog) inventorying dotfiles
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "whoami" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "config list" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "config get"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the originating npm/pip install command line and the package being installed; correlate against advisory feeds for known-compromised versions in the last 24h. 2) Contain: rotate npm/PyPI publishing tokens for the affected user, revoke any GitHub PATs scoped from the same machine, and quarantine the endpoint pending image rebuild. 3) Hunt: check npm/PyPI registry audit logs for publishes from the user's account in the last 7 days, search the fleet for additional installs of the same package@version, and verify cooldown policy is now enforced on the user's package-manager config.
let creds = dynamic([".npmrc",".yarnrc",".yarnrc.yml","bunfig.toml",".pypirc","pip.conf"]);
let pmParents = dynamic(["npm.exe","npm-cli.js","pnpm.exe","yarn.exe","bun.exe","node.exe","pip.exe","pip3.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","npm","pip","node","python","python3"]);
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ (creds)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (pmParents) or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ (pmParents)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
let creds = dynamic([".npmrc",".yarnrc",".yarnrc.yml","bunfig.toml",".pypirc","pip.conf"]);
let pmParents = dynamic(["npm.exe","npm-cli.js","pnpm.exe","yarn.exe","bun.exe","node.exe","pip.exe","pip3.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","npm","pip","node","python","python3"]);
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFileName in~ (creds)
| where ActingProcessName in~ (pmParents) or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (pmParents)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, EventType
title: Package Manager Descendant Reads Registry Credentials
id: f5d76a82-3a8d-44e6-b7ef-13c69e2e6451
description: Reads of .npmrc, .yarnrc, bunfig.toml, .pypirc, pip.conf by npm/pnpm/yarn/bun/pip/node/python — the harvest step in Miasma/Hades worm chains.
references:
  - https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/prevent-npm-and-python-supply-chain-attacks-on-developer-machines-with-package-configs
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/16
tags:
  - attack.t1552.001
  - attack.credential_access
logsource:
  category: file_access
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_file:
    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - '\.npmrc'
      - '\.yarnrc'
      - '\.yarnrc.yml'
      - '\bunfig.toml'
      - '\.pypirc'
      - '\pip.conf'
  selection_parent:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\node.exe'
      - '\npm.exe'
      - '\pnpm.exe'
      - '\yarn.exe'
      - '\bun.exe'
      - '\python.exe'
      - '\python3.exe'
      - '\pip.exe'
      - '\pip3.exe'
  condition: selection_file and selection_parent
level: medium
source:(windows.sysmon OR linux.auditd) (@TargetFilename:(*\\.npmrc OR *\\.yarnrc OR *\\.yarnrc.yml OR *\\bunfig.toml OR *\\.pypirc OR *\\pip.conf) OR @file.path:(*/.npmrc OR */.yarnrc OR */.yarnrc.yml OR */bunfig.toml OR */.pypirc OR */pip.conf)) (@Image:(*\\node.exe OR *\\npm.exe OR *\\pnpm.exe OR *\\yarn.exe OR *\\bun.exe OR *\\python.exe OR *\\python3.exe OR *\\pip.exe OR *\\pip3.exe) OR @process.executable.path:(*/node OR */npm OR */pnpm OR */yarn OR */bun OR */python* OR */pip*))
#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo
| TargetFileName=/(\\\.npmrc|\\\.yarnrc(\.yml)?|\\bunfig\.toml|\\\.pypirc|\\pip\.conf|\/\.npmrc|\/\.yarnrc(\.yml)?|\/bunfig\.toml|\/\.pypirc|\/pip\.conf)$/i
| ContextImageFileName=/(\\|\/)(node|npm|pnpm|yarn|bun|python3?|pip3?)(\.exe)?$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name IN (".npmrc",".yarnrc",".yarnrc.yml","bunfig.toml",".pypirc","pip.conf")) by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.process_path Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.action | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | search process_path IN ("*\\node.exe","*\\python.exe","*\\python3","*\\pip*","*\\npm*","*\\yarn*","*\\pnpm*","*\\bun*","*/node","*/python*","*/pip*") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name IN (".npmrc",".yarnrc",".yarnrc.yml","bunfig.toml",".pypirc","pip.conf")) by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.process_path Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.action | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | search process_path IN ("*\\node.exe","*\\python.exe","*\\python3","*\\pip*","*\\npm*","*\\yarn*","*\\pnpm*","*\\bun*","*/node","*/python*","*/pip*") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Post-install node or python child process beaconing to non-registry public destination AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts for node/python (descended from an npm or pip install) making outbound network connections to public destinations that are NOT the legitimate package registries — the egress channel a Miasma/Hades post-install script would use to exfil harvested tokens or pull the next stage. Article-specific because it pivots on the install-time parent chain plus the explicit registry destination set named in the article. Rationale: Article identifies the public registries as the legitimate egress endpoints ("registry is their highway") — any node/python descended from an install talking to anything else is the suspicious shape. Sentinel variant restructured to use SrcHostname (per validator suggestion) and an ImProcessCreate prefilter for hosts running the install chain, since ImDnsActivity lacks a process column. Cross-checked StepSecurity write-up and MITRE T1071.001. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/prevent-npm-and-python-supply-chain-attacks-on-developer-machines-with-package-configs • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1071/001/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Package post-install script legitimately fetching binary deps from GitHub Releases or npmjs.com (e.g. esbuild, prebuild-install, node-gyp downloading prebuilt binaries)
  • Telemetry/error reporting from packages like sentry-cli or pytest-sentry
  • Developer running npx of a script that legitimately calls a SaaS API
  • Internal package post-install that reaches the corporate license server (catch by allowing *.internal)
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteUrl has_any ("github.com","githubusercontent.com","objects.githubusercontent.com") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("prebuild-install","node-gyp","esbuild"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the install command line, package@version, and the post-install script (look in node_modules/<pkg>/package.json `scripts.postinstall` or setup.py); reverse the destination domain via WHOIS / passive DNS. 2) Contain: kill the install process, rotate the user's npm and PyPI tokens, block the destination at the proxy, and snapshot ~/.npmrc and ~/.pypirc before image rebuild. 3) Hunt: search the fleet for any other endpoint that DNS-resolved the same destination in the last 14 days, pivot to npm/PyPI publish events under the user's tokens for republished tarballs, and verify the bad package@version is now blocked at the internal mirror.
let pmAncestors = dynamic(["npm.exe","pnpm.exe","yarn.exe","bun.exe","pip.exe","pip3.exe","npm","pip"]);
let allowedRegistries = dynamic(["registry.npmjs.org","registry.yarnpkg.com","pypi.org","files.pythonhosted.org","npm.pkg.github.com"]);
let installers = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(1d)
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (pmAncestors) or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ (pmAncestors)
    | where FileName in~ ("node.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","node","python","python3")
    | project InstallTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, InstallerPid = ProcessId, InstallerName = FileName, InstallerCmd = ProcessCommandLine;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","node","python","python3")
| where not (RemoteUrl has_any (allowedRegistries))
| join kind=inner installers on $left.DeviceId == $right.DeviceId, $left.InitiatingProcessId == $right.InstallerPid
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, InstallTime, InstallerCmd
| order by Timestamp desc
let allowedRegistries = dynamic(["registry.npmjs.org","registry.yarnpkg.com","pypi.org","files.pythonhosted.org","npm.pkg.github.com"]);
let endpointHosts = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
    | where ParentProcessName has_any ("npm","pnpm","yarn","bun","pip","pip3")
    | where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","python","python3")
    | summarize by DvcHostname;
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where SrcHostname in (endpointHosts)
| where not (DnsQuery has_any (allowedRegistries))
| where DnsQuery !endswith ".internal" and DnsQuery !endswith ".corp" and DnsQuery !endswith ".local"
| where DnsResponseCodeName == "NOERROR" or isempty(DnsResponseCodeName)
| summarize ResolvedHits = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), Domains = make_set(DnsQuery, 50) by SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr
| order by FirstSeen desc
source:(windows.sysmon OR linux.auditd) @EventID:3 (@Image:(*\\node.exe OR *\\python.exe OR *\\python3.exe) OR @process.executable.path:(*/node OR */python OR */python3)) -@DestinationHostname:(*registry.npmjs.org OR *registry.yarnpkg.com OR *pypi.org OR *files.pythonhosted.org OR *npm.pkg.github.com OR *.internal OR *.corp OR *.local)
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4
| ContextImageFileName=/(\\|\/)(node|python3?)(\.exe)?$/i

A Forgotten Contributor Account Compromised the Entire Mastra npm Package Scope

Snyk
2026-06-16 13 use cases 7 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A dormant contributor account was used to republish the entire @mastra npm scope, each injected with a single dependency, easy-day-js, that drops a cross-platform cryptocurrency stealer. Here is how the attack worked, how to check exposure, and how to remediate.

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — A Forgotten Contributor Account Compromised the Entire Mastra npm Package Scope
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] easy-day-js postinstall marker files (.pkg_history / .pkg_logs) created in user profile · [LLM] Windows persistence drop under C:\ProgramData\NodePackages by node/PowerShell · Suspicious browser extension installation · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Mastra npm supply chain — outbound connection to attacker IPs 23.254.164.92 / .123 · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Node.js process reading Chromium browser wallet/profile data (Mastra stealer) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process
Mastra npm supply chain — outbound connection to attacker IPs 23.254.164.92 / .123 AICommand & Control High
Hunts any host contacting the Hostwinds-hosted dropper IP (23.254.164.92:8000) or the RAT C2 (23.254.164.123) used by the easy-day-js postinstall payload from the June 2026 @mastra scope takeover. Either IP is article-specific and should not see any benign enterprise traffic. Rationale: Both IPs are named in the article (dropper 23.254.164.92:8000, RAT C2 23.254.164.123/49890878) and serve only this campaign on Hostwinds infra — pure IOC hit, near-zero benign baseline. Port 8000 + the 10-min beacon cadence add corroborating context the analyst can confirm.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel scanning appliances (e.g. RecordedFuture, GreyNoise sensors) deliberately reaching campaign infrastructure
  • SOC analyst sandbox detonations or malware reversers from a known forensic workstation
  • VPN exit nodes that happen to share the Hostwinds /24 (rare — verify with reverse DNS)
  • Legitimate Hostwinds-hosted customer service if any internal app coincidentally pins these IPs (validate against asset inventory)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("nmap.exe","masscan.exe","zgrab.exe") or DeviceName has_any ("sandbox","ti-collector","malware-lab"))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull the full DeviceNetworkEvents record; correlate InitiatingProcessFileName/CommandLine and check for node.exe/npm.exe parent within ±5 min. Pull the host's package-lock.json mtime to confirm if a recent npm install ran. Step 2 — Contain: isolate the host via Defender Live Response or EDR network containment; revoke any AWS/cloud session tokens, wallet seed phrases, and SSH keys readable by the user account. Treat the host as a credential and crypto-wallet exposure event. Step 3 — Hunt: sweep the fleet for SHA256 221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf, files C:\ProgramData\NodePackages\*, ~/.pkg_history, ~/.pkg_logs, and any package-lock.json referencing easy-day-js.

| where RemoteIP in ("23.254.164.92", "23.254.164.123")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| extend Note = case(RemoteIP == "23.254.164.92", "easy-day-js postinstall dropper :8000", RemoteIP == "23.254.164.123", "second-stage RAT C2 (~10m beacon)", "unknown")
| order by Timestamp desc

easy-day-js postinstall marker files (.pkg_history / .pkg_logs) created in user profile AIInstallation High
Detects creation of the dropper's install-tracking marker files (~/.pkg_history and ~/.pkg_logs) written by setup.cjs during the malicious postinstall hook. Filename pair is unique to this campaign and is written before the dropper self-deletes. Rationale: Filename pair (~/.pkg_history + ~/.pkg_logs) is verbatim from the dropper analysis and has no legitimate npm/node usage. Pairing with node/npm as the writing process eliminates the only realistic FP source (a user manually creating these files). The pair tag is unique to this campaign.
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007 T1070.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer experimentally creating files matching these names (extremely rare)
  • A second npm package coincidentally named pkg-history / pkg-logs creating its own dotfiles (validate by reading file contents)
  • Internal CI image pre-warming step that touches these paths (verify against build agent inventory)
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: inspect file contents (the dropper writes timestamps to track installs); list the host's npm install history from the last 24h and the resolved easy-day-js version. Step 2 — Contain: isolate host; rotate credentials accessible to the affected user (browser-saved passwords, SSH keys, AWS profiles, npm/GitHub tokens); seed-phrase rotation if a wallet is installed. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot to UC1 (outbound to 23.254.164.92/.123), enumerate every package-lock.json on the host for easy-day-js@1.11.21 or 1.11.22, and any @mastra/* version published on/after 2026-06-17.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified")
| where FileName in~ (".pkg_history",".pkg_logs")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","node","npm","yarn","pnpm.exe","pnpm")
   or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","npm-cli.js","yarn","pnpm.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFileName in~ (".pkg_history",".pkg_logs")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","npm","yarn","pnpm")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Windows persistence drop under C:\ProgramData\NodePackages by node/PowerShell AIInstallation High
Detects file creation under C:\ProgramData\NodePackages\* — the Windows persistence staging location used by the easy-day-js second-stage RAT, disguised as Node tooling. The path is article-specific and not produced by any legitimate Node.js installer (those use %APPDATA%\npm or %ProgramFiles%\nodejs). Rationale: C:\ProgramData\NodePackages is the exact persistence path called out in the article and is not used by official Node.js, npm, pnpm, or yarn installers (those live in %ProgramFiles% or %AppData%). A first-time write under this directory is a near-perfect IOC for the campaign's Windows persistence stage.
ATT&CKT1547.001 T1036.005 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A third-party Node-based product coincidentally choosing this directory name (audit installed-app inventory)
  • Internal packaging team using NodePackages as a custom ProgramData subdirectory (validate with platform team)
  • An EDR/MDM agent installer that pre-creates this path during deployment (rare — verify signer)
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: enumerate every file under C:\ProgramData\NodePackages including SHA256s; check schtasks /query, Run keys, and Services for any reference to the path. Step 2 — Contain: isolate; remove the directory after acquisition; revoke user credentials and any cloud session tokens; if a wallet is present, treat as compromised. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot to UC1/UC2; sweep the fleet for SHA256 221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf and for AsepValueUpdate / RegistryValueSet events pointing into this directory (the persistence anchor).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath startswith @"C:\ProgramData\NodePackages"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath startswith @"C:\ProgramData\NodePackages"
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Node.js process reading Chromium browser wallet/profile data (Mastra stealer) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts for node.exe / node touching Chromium browser profile artifacts — Local Extension Settings, Login Data, Cookies, Web Data — which is the file access pattern of the easy-day-js stealer payload. Node legitimately does not read live browser profiles; this is the read-side signature of the wallet-stealer stage. Rationale: Article explicitly states the stealer reads Chrome/Brave/Edge profiles for MetaMask, Phantom, Solflare, Coinbase, OKX and Keplr — all of which store data under \Local Extension Settings\ and \Login Data. Node.exe touching those paths is highly anomalous outside Electron/dev tooling (which we filter on the parent). Sigma omitted because the detection logically needs a process+path+parent-exclusion shape better expressed inline.
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1539 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Electron-based dev tools shelling out via node.exe to read their own profile cache (filtered on parent)
  • Browser-automation frameworks (Puppeteer, Playwright) used by QA engineers — typically point to a non-default user-data-dir; verify cmdline
  • Password-import or browser-migration utilities run interactively
  • Crypto-wallet dev/test fixtures using node to seed extension storage in a CI sandbox
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "--user-data-dir" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "puppeteer" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "playwright"
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: capture the node.exe command line and parent — Puppeteer/Playwright runs will pass --user-data-dir; a campaign hit will not. Pull listed installed wallet extensions and recent browser activity. Step 2 — Contain: isolate the host; assume seed phrases and browser-saved credentials are exfiltrated; immediately rotate session cookies on critical SaaS (AWS, GitHub, Slack), force re-auth, and instruct user to move crypto funds out of any browser-extension wallet using a clean device. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot to UC1 for outbound C2; check for the .pkg_history/.pkg_logs marker (UC2) and the C:\ProgramData\NodePackages persistence path (UC3) to confirm the dropper chain.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe"
| where FolderPath has_any (
    @"\Google\Chrome\User Data",
    @"\BraveSoftware\Brave-Browser\User Data",
    @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data"
  )
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","Web Data","Login Data For Account") or FolderPath has @"\Local Extension Settings\"
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("electron.exe","code.exe","slack.exe","discord.exe","teams.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node.exe","node")
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data",@"\BraveSoftware\Brave-Browser\User Data",@"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","Web Data") or TargetFilePath has @"\Local Extension Settings\"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:(windows.sysmon OR windows.defender) @EventID:11 (@Image:(*\\node.exe OR *\\Node.exe OR *\\NODE.EXE)) (@TargetFilename:*\\Local\ Extension\ Settings\\* OR @TargetFilename:*\\Login\ Data* OR @TargetFilename:*\\Cookies* OR @TargetFilename:*\\Web\ Data*)
(#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo OR #event_simpleName=FileWritten) ContextImageFileName=/\\node\.exe$/i
| regex("(Google\\\\Chrome\\\\User Data|BraveSoftware\\\\Brave-Browser\\\\User Data|Microsoft\\\\Edge\\\\User Data)", field=TargetFileName, flags="i")
| regex("(Local Extension Settings|Login Data|Cookies|Web Data)", field=TargetFileName, flags="i")
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=[count(as=Hits), min(_time, as=FirstSeen)])
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.process_name IN ("node.exe","node") AND (Filesystem.file_path="*\\Local Extension Settings\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Login Data*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Cookies*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Web Data*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.action
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.process_name IN ("node.exe","node") AND (Filesystem.file_path="*\\Local Extension Settings\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Login Data*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Cookies*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Web Data*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.action
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows

    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high

        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"

        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] LobeHub /webapi/proxy SSRF body targets internal IP or cloud-metadata endpoint · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer). → [LLM] Vulnerable LobeHub <=2.1.56 in Defender / Sentinel vulnerability inventory
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] LobeHub /webapi/proxy POST from scripted / non-browser User-Agent · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] LobeHub /webapi/proxy response reflects Clerk session cookie with Domain=lobehub.com · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Article-specific behavioural hunt — [GHSA / CRITICAL] CVE-2026-54157: LobeHub: Unauthenticated SSRF in `/webapi/prox
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Self-hosted LobeHub node process making outbound to internal / metadata IP (post-exploit SSRF)
LobeHub /webapi/proxy POST from scripted / non-browser User-Agent AIDelivery High
Detects unauthenticated POST requests to LobeHub's CVE-2026-54157 SSRF endpoint (`/webapi/proxy`) issued by curl/wget/python/PowerShell clients. Legitimate traffic to this route comes from the LobeHub web UI inside a browser; CLI / library user-agents touching it are extremely likely to be exploitation attempts. Rationale: Article shows the working PoC is `curl -X POST ... https://app.lobehub.com/webapi/proxy` — the endpoint is reachable from CLI without any auth, so attacker traffic shape will always be scripted-client UA. The LobeHub web UI invokes this from in-browser JS, so any non-browser UA on this exact path is high-fidelity exploitation. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xmwj-c75x-6346
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal synthetic monitoring (Datadog Synthetics, Pingdom, Site24x7) probing the proxy endpoint as a health-check
  • CI/CD release-validation scripts using curl/python-requests against staging LobeHub
  • Security team's own SSRF mitigation tests against patched instances
  • Third-party LobeHub SDKs / mobile apps that send a non-browser UA
Suppression filter
| where RequestClientApplication !has "DatadogSynthetics" and RequestClientApplication !has "Pingdom" and RequestClientApplication !has "Site24x7"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full POST body and check whether the URL the attacker proxied targets internal IPs, cloud metadata (169.254.169.254), or returned a reflected Set-Cookie — those upgrade severity instantly. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the edge / WAF and, on the LobeHub side, confirm package version is >2.1.56 with the `checkAuth()` patch applied; if not, hot-patch by adding the auth wrapper or removing the route. 3) Hunt: pivot on `SourceIP` for additional `/webapi/proxy` POSTs, search Clerk auth logs for `__session` values that match any reflected cookie, and review egress from LobeHub server IP for unexpected outbound during the same window.
let suspicious_ua = dynamic(["curl","wget","python-requests","python-urllib","go-http-client","powershell","httpie","libwww","java/","axios","node-fetch","nuclei","ffuf","gobuster"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has "lobehub.com/webapi/proxy"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe","opera.exe","iexplore.exe","safari.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
let suspicious_ua = dynamic(["curl","wget","python-requests","python-urllib","go-http-client","powershell","httpie","libwww","java/","axios","node-fetch","nuclei","ffuf","gobuster"]);
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestURL has "/webapi/proxy"
| where RequestMethod =~ "POST"
| extend ua = tolower(RequestClientApplication)
| where ua has_any (suspicious_ua) or isempty(ua) or ua == "-"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestMethod, RequestClientApplication
| order by TimeGenerated desc

description: Detects POST requests to the unauthenticated LobeHub /webapi/proxy SSRF endpoint coming from CLI / library user-agents rather than browsers.

  selection_ua:
    cs-User-Agent|contains:
      - 'curl/'

LobeHub /webapi/proxy SSRF body targets internal IP or cloud-metadata endpoint AIReconnaissance High
Detects POST requests to LobeHub's `/webapi/proxy` whose body URL points at RFC1918 internal ranges, loopback, `169.254.169.254` (AWS IMDS), `metadata.google.internal`, `metadata.azure.com`, or `file://`. These are the canonical SSRF targets attackers will pivot to once they discover the unauthenticated proxy. Rationale: Article PoC explicitly demonstrates POST-body URL fetching, and the GHSA confirms the only filter is `ssrfSafeFetch` — which historically has been bypassed via DNS rebinding and IPv6 mapping. Attacker bodies hitting metadata/loopback are the canonical post-discovery move; legitimate URL-preview traffic targets public domains only. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xmwj-c75x-6346
ATT&CKT1190 T1526 T1595.002
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorised pentest or bug-bounty researcher re-testing the SSRF fix
  • Internal red team exercise scoped to the LobeHub asset
  • Misconfigured client app accidentally sending an internal hostname in the URL preview
  • Security scanner (Nuclei, Burp) running an SSRF template in a maintenance window
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the exact SSRF target URL from the POST body and the HTTP response code/size — non-zero bodies returning AWS metadata JSON (`AccessKeyId`, `SecretAccessKey`) is an active credential-theft incident. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the edge, rotate any IAM role credentials attached to the LobeHub Vercel/EC2 identity, and upgrade LobeHub to >2.1.56 immediately. 3) Hunt: pull all CloudTrail events for the role/instance within the SSRF window for new credential use, search for the same source IP attempting other `/webapi/*` paths, and review for `__session` / `__clerk_db_jwt` cookie reflection (UC3).

| where RequestMethod =~ "POST"
| where Message has_any (ssrf_patterns)
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestMethod, RequestClientApplication, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

LobeHub /webapi/proxy response reflects Clerk session cookie with Domain=lobehub.com AIExploitation High
Detects the response-side signature of the CVE-2026-54157 cookie-injection chain: `/webapi/proxy` reflects an attacker-controlled `Set-Cookie` whose name matches Clerk's auth cookies (`__session`, `__clerk_db_jwt`, `__client_uat`) and whose `Domain=` is `lobehub.com`. This is the session-fixation primitive against logged-in users. Rationale: Article's second PoC is a direct demonstration: the proxy reflects upstream `Set-Cookie: __session=malicious;Domain=lobehub.com` verbatim — only `Content-Encoding` and `Content-Length` are stripped. Clerk's three documented cookies (`__session`, `__clerk_db_jwt`, `__client_uat`) being set on `lobehub.com` from the proxy route can only happen via this bug. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xmwj-c75x-6346 • https://clerk.com/docs/security/cookies
ATT&CKT1539 T1606.001
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • LobeHub's own Clerk auth endpoints legitimately issuing these cookies (different path — `/api/auth/*`, not `/webapi/proxy`)
  • Misconfigured upstream the proxy is fetching that coincidentally sets unrelated cookies named similarly
  • QA / staging environment intentionally injecting test cookies via the proxy
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the reflected cookie value and the source IP that triggered the response — note any victim browser IPs in adjacent `/webapi/proxy` interactions that may have stored the cookie. 2) Contain: invalidate Clerk sessions matching the reflected `__session` / `__clerk_db_jwt` values (Clerk Dashboard → Sessions → Revoke), block the source IP, and force `checkAuth()` patch via emergency LobeHub upgrade. 3) Hunt: pull Clerk audit logs for sign-ins that used the fixed cookie value, review subsequent privileged actions on those accounts, and search webserver logs for repeated proxy POSTs from referrer pages outside `app.lobehub.com` (CSRF stage).
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestURL has "/webapi/proxy"
| where Message has "Set-Cookie"
| where Message has_any ("__session","__clerk_db_jwt","__client_uat")
| where Message matches regex @"(?i)Domain=\.?lobehub\.com"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestMethod, RequestClientApplication, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Self-hosted LobeHub node process making outbound to internal / metadata IP (post-exploit SSRF) AIActions on Objectives Medium
For organisations running the npm `@lobehub/lobehub` package (≤2.1.56) on their own hosts: detects the LobeHub node.js server process initiating outbound connections to RFC1918 ranges, loopback, or cloud-metadata endpoints — the host-side smoking gun of CVE-2026-54157 being exploited against a self-hosted instance. Rationale: Article flags the npm package `@lobehub/lobehub <=2.1.56` is affected, meaning self-hosted deployments running node.js are in scope. Article also confirms the proxy reaches Vercel's management plane — on customer deployments, the equivalent target is the IMDS / private network. Outbound from the LobeHub node process to RFC1918 or 169.254.169.254 is the host-side fingerprint. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xmwj-c75x-6346 • https://www.npmjs.com/package/@lobehub/lobehub
ATT&CKT1526 T1552.005
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Node.js HTTP client legitimately calling internal microservices (Redis, internal API)
  • cloud-init / SSM Agent / IMDSv2 credential refresh from the same host (different process)
  • Container orchestrator probes from the node sidecar against link-local
  • Self-hosted LobeHub instance with a documented internal proxy/RAG backend at an RFC1918 address
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "healthcheck" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "--prometheus"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the source host is running `@lobehub/lobehub` (check package.json / running process command line) and that the destination is not a known internal microservice. Pull the upstream WAF/proxy log for matching `/webapi/proxy` POSTs in the same time window. 2) Contain: isolate the LobeHub host, rotate any IAM role / service-account credentials reachable from its metadata endpoint, and upgrade to >2.1.56 before re-attaching to network. 3) Hunt: search cloud audit logs (CloudTrail / Azure Activity / GCP audit) for API calls using credentials originating from the LobeHub instance role within the SSRF window; review egress for the same node PID making subsequent calls.

Vulnerable LobeHub <=2.1.56 in Defender / Sentinel vulnerability inventory AIWeaponization High
Asset-level detection: surfaces hosts where Defender's vulnerability inventory has identified CVE-2026-54157 (LobeHub `@lobehub/lobehub` ≤2.1.56). Pairs the finding with internet-exposure metadata so SOC can prioritise externally-reachable instances first. Rationale: Article specifies affected versions: `npm:@lobehub/lobehub <=2.1.56`. CveId match plus version-range regex provides a definitive asset hit. Joining DeviceInfo for `IsInternetFacing` lets the SOC prioritise the public-facing instances that the unauthenticated SSRF can be exploited against without any pre-existing access. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xmwj-c75x-6346 • https://www.npmjs.com/package/@lobehub/lobehub
