Vertex AI model deployed with artifactUri pointing to externally-owned GCS bucket AIInstallation High
Detects Vertex AI Model.deploy / DeployedModel registry entries whose underlying model artifactUri resolves to a Cloud Storage bucket not owned by the calling project's organisation. Catches post-hijack persistence — the squatted model survives the race condition only if it's then served, so a deploy referencing a foreign bucket is the smoking gun. Rationale: Article: 'When Vertex AI later loaded the swapped model, the attacker's code executed inside the serving container.' Deployment of a model whose artifactUri retains the pre-uuid4 vulnerable pattern (no UUID component) and lives in a foreign bucket is the persistence-of-hijack signature. Cross-checked against Unit 42's article — they explicitly enumerate the post-exploit damage (BigQuery, GKE, container images, internal tenant logs) reachable from the stolen token, which underscores why catching this at deploy-time matters. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/hijacking-vertex-ai-model/
ATT&CKT1525 T1036.005 T1199
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Multi-project ML platform legitimately promoting models from a central artifact registry project
  • Use of public Vertex AI Model Garden references that resolve to gs:// URIs in google-owned public buckets
  • Disaster-recovery restore deploying from a previously-archived bucket that retained the old naming
  • Federated research project where partner organisation legitimately owns the staging bucket
  • Legacy Vertex AI projects whose default bucket was created pre-v1.144.0 and never re-issued
Suppression filter
and not (@protoPayload.response.artifactUri:(gs://your-org-modelregistry-* OR gs://your-org-mlplatform-shared-*) OR @protoPayload.response.artifactUri:gs://cloud-samples-data/*)
Response runbook
1) Triage: resolve `dest_bucket` to its owning project via `gcloud storage buckets describe gs://<bucket> --format='value(projectNumber)'` and check organisation membership via Cloud Asset Inventory. Foreign org → confirmed compromise. 2) Contain: immediately UndeployModel on the affected Endpoint, then revoke the Vertex AI service agent's token via `gcloud iam service-accounts keys revoke` and force `gcloud auth application-default revoke` on any host that may have cached it; treat the serving container's BigQuery, GKE node SA, and KMS keys as compromised and rotate. 3) Hunt: search BigQuery jobs, GKE container.images.list, and KMS Decrypt audit logs for any call within 24h whose `principalEmail` matches the Vertex AI service agent and `callerIp` is outside Google's published service-agent ranges — that's the data-exfil window the article describes (BigQuery metadata, access lists, tenant logs, GKE cluster names, internal container image paths).
title: Vertex AI Model Deployed With Externally-Owned ArtifactUri
id: 7c4f8d12-9e3a-4b65-a2d8-1f0b3c8e9a47
status: experimental
description: Detects deployment of a Vertex AI model whose artifactUri references a Cloud Storage bucket outside the calling project — the persistence signature of the 'Pickle in the Middle' bucket-squatting attack.
references:
    - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/google-vertex-ai-sdk-flaw-let-attackers.html
    - https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/hijacking-vertex-ai-model/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/17

level: high

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-2473")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Article-specific behavioural hunt — Steam Workshop abused to spread malware via Wallpaper Engine app
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Wallpaper Engine spawning unexpected child process from Steam Workshop content directory · [LLM] AggregatorHost.dll loaded from non-System32 path (Steam credential stealer sideload) · [LLM] Known DarkKomet / Wallpaper-Engine campaign payload hash execution or write · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Outbound connection to Steam Workshop wallpaper campaign C2 (202.144.192.29 / 120.48.156.17 / brightly.to) · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Non-Steam process reading Steam sentry / loginusers credential files · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Wallpaper Engine spawning unexpected child process from Steam Workshop content directory AIInstallation High
Detects Wallpaper Engine (wallpaper32.exe / wallpaper64.exe) spawning a child process whose image resides under the Steam Workshop content directory for Wallpaper Engine (app id 431960). Per Kaspersky, malicious 'application'-type wallpapers auto-execute bundled payloads at install — this is the core execution telemetry shape. Rationale: Pulls the article's specific parent binaries (Wallpaper Engine's wallpaper32.exe/wallpaper64.exe) and the Wallpaper Engine Steam Workshop app id 431960 path. Cross-checked Steam app id from public Steam Wallpaper Engine page and SteamDB. Cross-checked against: • https://store.steampowered.com/app/431960/Wallpaper_Engine/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/002/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate 'application' wallpapers (system monitors, widget apps) installed by power users that the security team has not vetted
  • Wallpaper Engine self-update spawning its own installer from the Steam apps directory (parent path mismatch but similar shape)
  • Crash reporting via WerFault.exe being launched from the Workshop content folder
  • Developers testing their own Workshop submissions on dev workstations
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName in~ ("WerFault.exe","WerFaultSecure.exe","dllhost.exe") and InitiatingProcessParentFileName =~ "services.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the ChildImage SHA256/MD5 and cross-reference against the article's MD5 list and threat-intel; pull the Workshop content sub-folder (the numeric id after 431960 is the Workshop item id — look it up on steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=<id> to see the wallpaper name/author). 2) Contain: isolate the host via Defender Live Response or EDR network containment, kill the child process tree, remove the Workshop subscription via steam://url/CommunityFilePage/<id> when ready. 3) Hunt: pivot on the SHA256/MD5 across the fleet for other hosts with the same wallpaper, then run UC2/UC3/UC4 (AggregatorHost.dll sideload, Steam credential file access, C2 IPs) against the same DeviceId for the next 24h to surface follow-on stages.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wallpaper32.exe","wallpaper64.exe")
| where FolderPath has @"\steamapps\workshop\content\431960\" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has @"\steamapps\workshop\content\431960\"
| where FileName !in~ ("wallpaper32.exe","wallpaper64.exe","webwallpaper32.exe","webwallpaper64.exe","conhost.exe","WerFault.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ParentImage=InitiatingProcessFolderPath, ParentCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ChildImage=FolderPath, ChildCmd=ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, MD5
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\wallpaper32.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "\\wallpaper64.exe"
| where NewProcessName has @"\steamapps\workshop\content\431960\" or CommandLine has @"\steamapps\workshop\content\431960\"
| where NewProcessName !endswith "\\wallpaper32.exe" and NewProcessName !endswith "\\wallpaper64.exe" and NewProcessName !endswith "\\conhost.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Wallpaper Engine Spawning Child From Steam Workshop Content Directory
id: 5d7b5e4a-8a13-4d57-9e2c-31b8f1c4b2d4
description: Detects Wallpaper Engine spawning a child process whose image lives under the Wallpaper Engine Steam Workshop content folder (app id 431960).
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/steam-workshop-abused-to-spread-malware-via-wallpaper-engine-app/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/16
tags:
  - attack.t1204.002
  - attack.t1195.002
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\wallpaper32.exe'
      - '\wallpaper64.exe'
  selection_path:
    Image|contains: '\steamapps\workshop\content\431960\'
  filter_legit:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\wallpaper32.exe'

level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\wallpaper32.exe OR *\wallpaper64.exe OR *\Wallpaper32.exe OR *\Wallpaper64.exe) (@Image:*\steamapps\workshop\content\431960\* OR @CommandLine:*\steamapps\workshop\content\431960\*) -@Image:(*\wallpaper32.exe OR *\wallpaper64.exe OR *\conhost.exe OR *\WerFault.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ParentBaseFileName=/wallpaper(32|64)\.exe$/i
| regex("\\\\steamapps\\\\workshop\\\\content\\\\431960\\\\", field=ImageFileName) OR regex("\\\\steamapps\\\\workshop\\\\content\\\\431960\\\\", field=CommandLine)
| NOT ImageFileName=/wallpaper(32|64)\.exe$/i
| NOT ImageFileName=/conhost\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, SHA256HashData], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmdline values(Processes.process_hash) as hashes values(Processes.user) as user from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("wallpaper32.exe","wallpaper64.exe") AND (Processes.process_path="*\\steamapps\\workshop\\content\\431960\\*" OR Processes.parent_process="*\\steamapps\\workshop\\content\\431960\\*") by Processes.dest Processes.process_name Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where process_name!="wallpaper32.exe" AND process_name!="wallpaper64.exe"
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmdline values(Processes.process_hash) as hashes values(Processes.user) as user from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("wallpaper32.exe","wallpaper64.exe") AND (Processes.process_path="*\\steamapps\\workshop\\content\\431960\\*" OR Processes.parent_process="*\\steamapps\\workshop\\content\\431960\\*") by Processes.dest Processes.process_name Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where process_name!="wallpaper32.exe" AND process_name!="wallpaper64.exe"
AggregatorHost.dll loaded from non-System32 path (Steam credential stealer sideload) AIInstallation High
Genuine AggregatorHost.dll ships in %WINDIR%\System32\. The article's payload bundles a same-named DLL outside System32 to blend in. Detects any process loading AggregatorHost.dll whose folder path is not the canonical System32 location. Rationale: Article names AggregatorHost.dll specifically as the sideloaded Steam credential stealer. Real AggregatorHost.dll is a tiny Windows .NET host stub in System32 — any other location is high-fidelity. MITRE T1574.002 mapping confirmed against attack.mitre.org. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1574/002/
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers running locally-built .NET-hosting code that names its host AggregatorHost.dll (very rare)
  • Software-deployment shares (SCCM, Intune Win32 app cache) staging the legitimate DLL under %ProgramData% before copy to System32
  • Restore/repair operations from Windows installation media mounting an offline image
  • Forensic tools or analysts running the DLL from a sandbox path during incident response
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msiexec.exe","trustedinstaller.exe","setup.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash the loaded DLL, compare SHA256/MD5 to the known-bad list in UC5, and check signature with sigcheck/Get-AuthenticodeSignature — genuine AggregatorHost.dll is Microsoft-signed; the malicious copy will be unsigned or signed by an unfamiliar publisher. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the loading process, quarantine the DLL file and its parent folder (likely a Workshop subfolder under steamapps\workshop\content\431960\). 3) Hunt: enumerate all DeviceFileEvents writes of AggregatorHost.dll in the last 30 days across the fleet, pivot on InitiatingProcessFileName to find every distinct dropper, and check for outbound network connections from the loading process to the article's C2 IPs.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "AggregatorHost.dll"
| where FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\System32\"
     and FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\SysWOW64\"
     and FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\WinSxS\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, SHA256, MD5, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
Event
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Source =~ "Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon" and EventID == 7
| extend ImageLoaded = tostring(parse_xml(EventData).EventData.Data[5].["#text"])
| extend ProcessImage = tostring(parse_xml(EventData).EventData.Data[4].["#text"])
| extend ImageHashes = tostring(parse_xml(EventData).EventData.Data[11].["#text"])
| where ImageLoaded endswith @"\AggregatorHost.dll"
| where ImageLoaded !startswith @"C:\Windows\System32\"
     and ImageLoaded !startswith @"C:\Windows\SysWOW64\"
     and ImageLoaded !startswith @"C:\Windows\WinSxS\"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessImage, ImageLoaded, ImageHashes
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: AggregatorHost.dll Loaded From Non-System32 Path (Wallpaper Engine Sideload)
id: a3f1c4b2-7d8e-4f9a-9b1c-2d4e5f6a7b8c
description: Detects load of AggregatorHost.dll from any folder other than the canonical System32 / SysWOW64 / WinSxS paths, a sideload technique observed in the Steam Workshop Wallpaper Engine credential-theft chain.
references:

#event_simpleName=ClassifiedModuleLoad OR #event_simpleName=ImageHash

Non-Steam process reading Steam sentry / loginusers credential files AIActions on Objectives High
Detects file reads or copies of Steam credential artefacts (ssfn* sentry files, loginusers.vdf, config.vdf) by processes that are not part of the Steam client family. The article calls out Steam account credential theft as the goal of the sideloaded AggregatorHost.dll. Rationale: ssfn* files are Steam's machine-binding sentry tokens — possession means session takeover without the password. loginusers.vdf holds the cached account list. Article explicitly states the goal is to 'search for Steam accounts on the computer and steal account credentials.' Cross-checked Steam credential artefact paths against public Steam Support documentation. Cross-checked against: • https://help.steampowered.com/en/faqs/view/65A9-CFE7-2369-A0A8 • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/
ATT&CKT1555 T1539 T1083
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Backup utilities (Acronis, Veeam Agent, Macrium) capturing user profile data including the Steam config folder
  • AV/EDR products scanning the Steam config folder during a full filesystem sweep
  • Steam beta launcher variants or third-party Steam family-sharing tools that legitimately read ssfn files
  • Forensic acquisition tools (FTK Imager, KAPE) being run by IR or sysadmins
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("backup.exe","veeamagent.exe","acronis_loader.exe","mscsweep.exe","MsMpEng.exe","kape.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify InitiatingProcessFileName and its SHA256; if it's an unsigned binary under steamapps\workshop\content\431960\ this is almost certainly the article's stealer. Grab a copy of the file for malware analysis. 2) Contain: isolate the host, force-log out the affected Steam account via Steam Account Security (deauthorize all devices), invalidate the user's Steam password and Steam Guard recovery codes, and remove the malicious wallpaper Workshop subscription. 3) Hunt: pivot on the dropper SHA256 across the fleet, query UC2 (AggregatorHost.dll sideload) and UC4 (C2 connections) for the same host, and check Steam community trade/market activity for the user's account in the last 7 days for asset theft.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
     or FolderPath has @"\Steam\config\"
| where FileName matches regex @"(?i)^(loginusers\.vdf|config\.vdf|ssfn[0-9]+)$"
     or FolderPath has @"\Steam\config\"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("steam.exe","steamservice.exe","steamwebhelper.exe","gameoverlayui.exe","streaming_client.exe","steamerrorreporter.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Steam\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFileName matches regex @"(?i)^(loginusers\.vdf|config\.vdf|ssfn[0-9]+)$"
   or TargetFilePath has @"\Steam\config\"
| where not (ActingProcessName has_any ("steam.exe","steamservice.exe","steamwebhelper.exe","gameoverlayui.exe","streaming_client.exe","steamerrorreporter.exe"))
| where not (ActingProcessCommandLine has @"\Steam\")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Non-Steam Process Accessing Steam Credential Artefacts
id: 7b9c1d2e-3f4a-5b6c-7d8e-9f0a1b2c3d4e
description: Detects file access to Steam sentry (ssfn*), loginusers.vdf, or config.vdf by processes outside the Steam client family — the credential-theft step of the Steam Workshop Wallpaper Engine campaign.
references:

author: SOC Detection Engineering

#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo OR #event_simpleName=FileWritten
| TargetFileName=/(\\loginusers\.vdf|\\config\.vdf|\\ssfn[0-9]+|\\Steam\\config\\)/i

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Filesystem.file_path) as file_path values(Filesystem.process_name) as process from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name="loginusers.vdf" OR Filesystem.file_name="config.vdf" OR Filesystem.file_name="ssfn*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where NOT match(process_name, "(?i)^(steam|steamservice|steamwebhelper|gameoverlayui|streaming_client)\.exe$")

Outbound connection to Steam Workshop wallpaper campaign C2 (202.144.192.29 / 120.48.156.17 / brightly.to) AICommand & Control High
Network beacon to the three article-named C2 endpoints used by the DarkKomet backdoor / AggregatorHost stealer / Lumma / Vidar / RanEngine payloads delivered through malicious Wallpaper Engine wallpapers. Any internal host contacting these is high-confidence compromise. Rationale: All three indicators are named directly in the kill-chain reconstruction for the same campaign and tied to multiple distinct payload families (DarkKomet, AggregatorHost, Lumma, Vidar, RanEngine). No second-source corroboration yet (campaign just published), so confidence relies on the Kaspersky attribution; treat any internal hit as a confirmed-compromise pivot.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel feed validation traffic from a security tool (e.g. analyst sandbox detonation hitting the C2)
  • Researcher VM intentionally browsing brightly.to for analysis
  • Shared-hosting provider parking the IP on an unrelated benign domain (verify reverse DNS)
  • Outbound proxy / SASE service health-checking a blocklisted URL
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","falcon-sensor.exe","sentinelagent.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify which internal hosts connected and which user/process initiated; pull InitiatingProcessFileName & InitiatingProcessFolderPath — if process lives under steamapps\workshop\content\431960\ this is the article's chain. 2) Contain: block 202.144.192.29, 120.48.156.17, and *.brightly.to at egress firewall + DNS sinkhole; isolate the originating hosts via EDR network containment; force-revoke Steam Guard tokens and reset Steam passwords for affected users. 3) Hunt: run UC1/UC2/UC3 across the same DeviceId for the previous 30 days, search DeviceFileEvents for the hashes in UC5, and pivot from the originating process SHA256 across the fleet to find any other host with the same dropper.
let C2_IPs = dynamic(["202.144.192.29","120.48.156.17"]);
let C2_Domains = dynamic(["brightly.to"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in (C2_IPs)
   or RemoteUrl has_any (C2_Domains)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
let C2_IPs = dynamic(["202.144.192.29","120.48.156.17"]);
let C2_Domains = dynamic(["brightly.to"]);
union isfuzzy=true
    (ImNetworkSession
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
        | where DstIpAddr in (C2_IPs) or DstHostname in~ (C2_Domains) or Url has_any (C2_Domains)
        | project TimeGenerated, Host=DvcHostname, User=SrcUsername, Process=tostring(parse_json("")), RemoteIP=DstIpAddr, RemoteUrl=coalesce(DstHostname, Url)),
    (ImDnsActivity
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
        | where DnsQuery in~ (C2_Domains)
        | project TimeGenerated, Host=DvcHostname, User=SrcUsername, Process="", RemoteIP="", RemoteUrl=DnsQuery),
    (CommonSecurityLog
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
        | where DestinationIP in (C2_IPs) or RequestURL has_any (C2_Domains) or DestinationDnsDomain has_any (C2_Domains)
        | project TimeGenerated, Host=SourceHostName, User=SourceUserName, Process=DestinationProcessName, RemoteIP=DestinationIP, RemoteUrl=coalesce(RequestURL, DestinationDnsDomain))
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Known DarkKomet / Wallpaper-Engine campaign payload hash execution or write AIInstallation Medium
Detects execution or file-write of any of the 13 article-named MD5s tied to the malicious wallpaper bundles (DarkKomet droppers, AggregatorHost.dll variants, Lumma/Vidar/RanEngine stages). Pure IOC hunt; will catch any host that downloaded a known-bad Workshop package even if behaviour-based UCs missed it. Rationale: All 13 MD5s are taken verbatim from the article's pre-extracted IOC bundle covering the DarkKomet droppers and AggregatorHost.dll sideload payloads. 90-day lookback because some Workshop subscriptions sit on disk for weeks before installation/launch.
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1027.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware-analysis sandbox or research VM in the fleet legitimately running known-bad samples
  • EDR / SOAR auto-detonation pipeline (e.g. ANY.RUN connector) leaving sample artefacts on a SOC host
  • Threat-intel vendor agent caching a sample for offline scanning
  • Old quarantine restore on an analyst workstation pulling a sample for reverse engineering
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm hit isn't an analyst sandbox; pull DeviceName, FolderPath, parent process and timeline of the file write — chase upstream to find the wallpaper Workshop item id (the path under steamapps\workshop\content\431960\<id>\). 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill any running process matching the hash, quarantine the file system-wide via Defender Indicator (FileHash → BlockAndRemediate), push the 13 hashes to corporate AV/EDR blocklists. 3) Hunt: run UC4 (C2 IPs) and UC3 (Steam credential file access) against the affected host for the last 90 days; submit the Workshop item id (and author Steam ID) to Valve security via steamcommunity.com/dev for takedown; query CrowdStrike / Defender across the fleet for any other host with these MD5s on disk even without execution.
let BadMD5 = dynamic(["95856f2ce428c728d9781d3296558068","af080780cca2acd1d082ce01e7cc346a","c133c3dd9f7d6934598025047df41abf","d1693bbff456ae8fa3360446706df6da","8c2cc585ad8a13a72a704c0fda0c9854","b9fa763a53da3eea742d0f3c845a8c09","ded08ae5df7f1b12e5fdb767dbbed0b1","20965254e29104986e11939decd39549","18dedc0009f0927cba6425c84cce9883","0f4f01c6d495abb37403072dd017ce8d","5620f01284329f561b1839a36be55355","fe1f6485013cd5e6d5cf718049b0b8d6","74414ed4b63aadec039b603c32762b80"]);
union isfuzzy=true
    (DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(90d)
        | where MD5 in (BadMD5) or InitiatingProcessMD5 in (BadMD5)
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Source="Process", FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, MD5, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath),
    (DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(90d)
        | where MD5 in (BadMD5)
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, Source="FileWrite", FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, MD5, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath),
    (DeviceImageLoadEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(90d)
        | where MD5 in (BadMD5)
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, Source="DllLoad", FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, MD5, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath=InitiatingProcessFolderPath)
| order by Timestamp desc
let BadMD5 = dynamic(["95856f2ce428c728d9781d3296558068","af080780cca2acd1d082ce01e7cc346a","c133c3dd9f7d6934598025047df41abf","d1693bbff456ae8fa3360446706df6da","8c2cc585ad8a13a72a704c0fda0c9854","b9fa763a53da3eea742d0f3c845a8c09","ded08ae5df7f1b12e5fdb767dbbed0b1","20965254e29104986e11939decd39549","18dedc0009f0927cba6425c84cce9883","0f4f01c6d495abb37403072dd017ce8d","5620f01284329f561b1839a36be55355","fe1f6485013cd5e6d5cf718049b0b8d6","74414ed4b63aadec039b603c32762b80"]);
union isfuzzy=true
    (ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
        | where MD5 in (BadMD5)
        | project TimeGenerated, Host=DvcHostname, User=ActorUsername, Source="Process", FileName=TargetProcessName, CommandLine=TargetProcessCommandLine, MD5, SHA256),
    (ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
        | where TargetFileMD5 in (BadMD5) or Hash in (BadMD5)
        | project TimeGenerated, Host=DvcHostname, User=ActorUsername, Source="FileEvent", FileName=TargetFileName, CommandLine=ActingProcessCommandLine, MD5=TargetFileMD5, SHA256=TargetFileSHA256),
    (SecurityEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)

        | where FileHash has_any (BadMD5)

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.

            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'

falsepositives:

level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("95856f2ce428c728d9781d3296558068", "af080780cca2acd1d082ce01e7cc346a", "c133c3dd9f7d6934598025047df41abf", "d1693bbff456ae8fa3360446706df6da", "8c2cc585ad8a13a72a704c0fda0c9854", "b9fa763a53da3eea742d0f3c845a8c09", "ded08ae5df7f1b12e5fdb767dbbed0b1", "20965254e29104986e11939decd39549", "18dedc0009f0927cba6425c84cce9883", "0f4f01c6d495abb37403072dd017ce8d", "5620f01284329f561b1839a36be55355", "fe1f6485013cd5e6d5cf718049b0b8d6", "74414ed4b63aadec039b603c32762b80") or SHA1 in~ ("95856f2ce428c728d9781d3296558068", "af080780cca2acd1d082ce01e7cc346a", "c133c3dd9f7d6934598025047df41abf", "d1693bbff456ae8fa3360446706df6da", "8c2cc585ad8a13a72a704c0fda0c9854", "b9fa763a53da3eea742d0f3c845a8c09", "ded08ae5df7f1b12e5fdb767dbbed0b1", "20965254e29104986e11939decd39549", "18dedc0009f0927cba6425c84cce9883", "0f4f01c6d495abb37403072dd017ce8d", "5620f01284329f561b1839a36be55355", "fe1f6485013cd5e6d5cf718049b0b8d6", "74414ed4b63aadec039b603c32762b80") or MD5 in~ ("95856f2ce428c728d9781d3296558068", "af080780cca2acd1d082ce01e7cc346a", "c133c3dd9f7d6934598025047df41abf", "d1693bbff456ae8fa3360446706df6da", "8c2cc585ad8a13a72a704c0fda0c9854", "b9fa763a53da3eea742d0f3c845a8c09", "ded08ae5df7f1b12e5fdb767dbbed0b1", "20965254e29104986e11939decd39549", "18dedc0009f0927cba6425c84cce9883", "0f4f01c6d495abb37403072dd017ce8d", "5620f01284329f561b1839a36be55355", "fe1f6485013cd5e6d5cf718049b0b8d6", "74414ed4b63aadec039b603c32762b80")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("95856f2ce428c728d9781d3296558068", "af080780cca2acd1d082ce01e7cc346a", "c133c3dd9f7d6934598025047df41abf", "d1693bbff456ae8fa3360446706df6da", "8c2cc585ad8a13a72a704c0fda0c9854", "b9fa763a53da3eea742d0f3c845a8c09", "ded08ae5df7f1b12e5fdb767dbbed0b1", "20965254e29104986e11939decd39549", "18dedc0009f0927cba6425c84cce9883", "0f4f01c6d495abb37403072dd017ce8d", "5620f01284329f561b1839a36be55355", "fe1f6485013cd5e6d5cf718049b0b8d6", "74414ed4b63aadec039b603c32762b80") or SHA1 in~ ("95856f2ce428c728d9781d3296558068", "af080780cca2acd1d082ce01e7cc346a", "c133c3dd9f7d6934598025047df41abf", "d1693bbff456ae8fa3360446706df6da", "8c2cc585ad8a13a72a704c0fda0c9854", "b9fa763a53da3eea742d0f3c845a8c09", "ded08ae5df7f1b12e5fdb767dbbed0b1", "20965254e29104986e11939decd39549", "18dedc0009f0927cba6425c84cce9883", "0f4f01c6d495abb37403072dd017ce8d", "5620f01284329f561b1839a36be55355", "fe1f6485013cd5e6d5cf718049b0b8d6", "74414ed4b63aadec039b603c32762b80") or MD5 in~ ("95856f2ce428c728d9781d3296558068", "af080780cca2acd1d082ce01e7cc346a", "c133c3dd9f7d6934598025047df41abf", "d1693bbff456ae8fa3360446706df6da", "8c2cc585ad8a13a72a704c0fda0c9854", "b9fa763a53da3eea742d0f3c845a8c09", "ded08ae5df7f1b12e5fdb767dbbed0b1", "20965254e29104986e11939decd39549", "18dedc0009f0927cba6425c84cce9883", "0f4f01c6d495abb37403072dd017ce8d", "5620f01284329f561b1839a36be55355", "fe1f6485013cd5e6d5cf718049b0b8d6", "74414ed4b63aadec039b603c32762b80")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["95856f2ce428c728d9781d3296558068", "af080780cca2acd1d082ce01e7cc346a", "c133c3dd9f7d6934598025047df41abf", "d1693bbff456ae8fa3360446706df6da", "8c2cc585ad8a13a72a704c0fda0c9854", "b9fa763a53da3eea742d0f3c845a8c09", "ded08ae5df7f1b12e5fdb767dbbed0b1", "20965254e29104986e11939decd39549", "18dedc0009f0927cba6425c84cce9883", "0f4f01c6d495abb37403072dd017ce8d", "5620f01284329f561b1839a36be55355", "fe1f6485013cd5e6d5cf718049b0b8d6", "74414ed4b63aadec039b603c32762b80"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] ClickFix Run-dialog PowerShell download chain (BabaDeda/Lorem Ipsum/Potemkin) · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] MSI installer spawning HTA payload (Potemkin delivery chain) · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — ClickFix Campaigns Expand Malware Delivery With New Loaders and Fake Update Lure
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Outdated Node.js v7.10.1 launched from user-writable path (Lorem Ipsum Loader) · [LLM] DLL side-load of mscoree.dll or msvcp140.dll from non-System32 path (Lorem Ipsum) · [LLM] Potemkin host-marker file %LOCALAPPDATA%\hyper-v.ver creation · [LLM] Storage Crypter external-storage payload read (BabaDeda List.Control.dat) · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
ClickFix Run-dialog PowerShell download chain (BabaDeda/Lorem Ipsum/Potemkin) AIDelivery Medium
Detects the ClickFix social-engineering entry point common to all three loader families: explorer.exe (Run dialog paste) spawning a hidden PowerShell that immediately downloads a ZIP, Node.js binary, MSI, or .dat staging payload. This pivots on parent=explorer because ClickFix tricks the user into pasting the attacker-supplied command into Win+R. Rationale: Article describes all three loader families (BabaDeda, Lorem Ipsum, Potemkin) using ClickFix to coerce users into pasting attacker-supplied PowerShell into the Run dialog — making parent=explorer.exe the strongest behavioural anchor. Cmdline tokens (Node.js, ZIP, MSI, HTA, .dat) match the staged delivery shapes described per family.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT admin pasting a winget/Chocolatey bootstrap into Win+R
  • Software deployment teams running adhoc PS one-liners that fetch internal MSIs
  • Developer test scripts launched manually from Run dialog with Invoke-WebRequest
  • Endpoint health-check scripts pushed via vendor docs ("paste this in Run")
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "winget" and ProcessCommandLine !has_any ("winget", "chocolatey", "choco install", "\\\\corp.local\\", "\\\\internal.")
Response runbook
Triage: Pull the full PS cmdline plus 5-minute child-process tail on the same host — look for node.exe, msiexec.exe, mshta.exe, or DLL side-load follow-ons. Resolve any URL in the cmdline against VT/URLhaus and check whether the host is education/finance (BabaDeda target sector) or recently visited a compromised WordPress site. Contain: Isolate the device via Defender Live Response if any follow-on stage 2 (Node.js from user path, mshta, rundll32 of side-loaded DLL) fired; kill the PS process tree; revoke recent user tokens. Hunt: Pivot on the user across the prior 24h for SEO-driven downloads, Edge "security update" lures in browser history, and other hosts that contacted the same C2 URL.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "explorer.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-w hidden", "-windowstyle hidden", "-WindowStyle h", "-nop", "-noprofile")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("DownloadFile", "Invoke-WebRequest", "iwr ", "Invoke-RestMethod", "irm ", "Invoke-Expression", "iex ", "curl ", "Start-BitsTransfer")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (".zip", "node", ".msi", ".dat", "mshta", ".hta")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\explorer.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\powershell.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("-w hidden", "-windowstyle hidden", "-WindowStyle h", "-nop", "-noprofile")
| where CommandLine has_any ("DownloadFile", "Invoke-WebRequest", "iwr ", "Invoke-RestMethod", "irm ", "Invoke-Expression", "iex ", "curl ", "Start-BitsTransfer")
| where CommandLine has_any (".zip", "node", ".msi", ".dat", "mshta", ".hta")
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: ClickFix Run-Dialog PowerShell Download Chain
id: 7f3e2a1b-9c4d-4e8a-b6f2-1d3c5e7a9b21
status: experimental
description: PowerShell launched from explorer.exe (Win+R Run-dialog paste) with a hidden window flag and an inline download cmdlet pulling a ZIP, Node.js, MSI, or .dat payload — the canonical ClickFix entry point used to drop BabaDeda, Lorem Ipsum, and Potemkin loaders.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/clickfix-campaigns-expand-malware.html
author: SOC Detection Team
date: 2026/06/17
tags:
  - attack.initial_access
  - attack.execution
  - attack.t1566.002
  - attack.t1204.001
  - attack.t1059.001
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith: '\explorer.exe'
  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
  selection_window:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '-w hidden'
      - '-windowstyle hidden'
      - '-WindowStyle h'
      - '-nop'
      - '-noprofile'
  selection_download:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'DownloadFile'
      - 'Invoke-WebRequest'
      - 'iwr '
      - 'Invoke-RestMethod'
      - 'irm '
      - 'Invoke-Expression'
      - 'iex '
      - 'Start-BitsTransfer'
  selection_payload:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '.zip'
      - 'node'
      - '.msi'
      - '.dat'
      - 'mshta'
      - '.hta'
  condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_window and selection_download and selection_payload
falsepositives:
  - IT admin Win+R PowerShell one-liners that download internal tooling
  - Software-deployment scripts run interactively from Run dialog
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\\explorer.exe OR *\\Explorer.EXE OR *\\EXPLORER.EXE) @Image:(*\\powershell.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\pwsh.exe) (@CommandLine:*hidden* OR @CommandLine:*-nop* OR @CommandLine:*-noprofile*) (@CommandLine:*DownloadFile* OR @CommandLine:*Invoke-WebRequest* OR @CommandLine:*iwr* OR @CommandLine:*Invoke-RestMethod* OR @CommandLine:*irm* OR @CommandLine:*Invoke-Expression* OR @CommandLine:*iex* OR @CommandLine:*Start-BitsTransfer*) (@CommandLine:*.zip* OR @CommandLine:*node* OR @CommandLine:*.msi* OR @CommandLine:*.dat* OR @CommandLine:*mshta* OR @CommandLine:*.hta*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/explorer\.exe$/i
| ImageFileName=/\\(powershell|pwsh)\.exe$/i
| CommandLine=/(?i)(-w\s+hidden|-windowstyle\s+hidden|-WindowStyle\s+h|-nop|-noprofile)/
| CommandLine=/(?i)(DownloadFile|Invoke-WebRequest|iwr\s|Invoke-RestMethod|irm\s|Invoke-Expression|iex\s|Start-BitsTransfer|curl\s)/
| CommandLine=/(?i)(\.zip|node|\.msi|\.dat|mshta|\.hta)/
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime FROM datamodel=Endpoint.Processes WHERE Processes.parent_process_name=explorer.exe AND Processes.process_name IN (powershell.exe, pwsh.exe) AND (Processes.process="*hidden*" OR Processes.process="* -nop *" OR Processes.process="*-windowstyle h*") AND (Processes.process="*DownloadFile*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-WebRequest*" OR Processes.process="*iwr *" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-RestMethod*" OR Processes.process="*irm *" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*" OR Processes.process="*iex *" OR Processes.process="*curl *") AND (Processes.process="*.zip*" OR Processes.process="*node*" OR Processes.process="*.msi*" OR Processes.process="*.dat*" OR Processes.process="*mshta*") BY Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process Processes.process Processes.process_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime FROM datamodel=Endpoint.Processes WHERE Processes.parent_process_name=explorer.exe AND Processes.process_name IN (powershell.exe, pwsh.exe) AND (Processes.process="*hidden*" OR Processes.process="* -nop *" OR Processes.process="*-windowstyle h*") AND (Processes.process="*DownloadFile*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-WebRequest*" OR Processes.process="*iwr *" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-RestMethod*" OR Processes.process="*irm *" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*" OR Processes.process="*iex *" OR Processes.process="*curl *") AND (Processes.process="*.zip*" OR Processes.process="*node*" OR Processes.process="*.msi*" OR Processes.process="*.dat*" OR Processes.process="*mshta*") BY Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process Processes.process Processes.process_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Outdated Node.js v7.10.1 launched from user-writable path (Lorem Ipsum Loader) AIInstallation High
Lorem Ipsum Loader's signature evasion: ships a 2017-era Node.js (v7.10.1) inside the ClickFix-delivered ZIP and uses it to execute the JavaScript payload, bypassing AV that whitelists modern signed node.exe. Hunts for any node.exe running from %TEMP%/%APPDATA%/Downloads with the legacy v7.x ProductVersion. Rationale: Article explicitly names "an outdated version of Node.js released in 2017 (version 7.10.1)" as the Lorem Ipsum Loader execution mechanism. Combination of node.exe + user-writable path is rare on corporate fleets — developers usually run from Program Files, AppData\Local\Programs\, or nvm directories with the current LTS.
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1218 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer running a portable Node.js extracted into a project folder under their user profile
  • Electron-based app (Slack, VS Code, Postman) running its embedded node helper from %APPDATA%
  • CI/CD agent or nvm-managed node interpreter under %APPDATA%\nvm\
  • npm install of native modules invoking node-gyp from project node_modules
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("slack.exe", "code.exe", "postman.exe", "discord.exe", "teams.exe") or FolderPath has_any (@"\AppData\Local\Programs\", @"\nvm\", @"\node_modules\"))
Response runbook
Triage: Read ProcessVersionInfoProductVersion — anything starting with 7.x is the Lorem Ipsum tell. Diff the SHA256 against the official Node.js v7.10.1 win-x64 release hash; check what JavaScript file was passed on the cmdline and where it sits on disk. Contain: Isolate the host, kill node.exe + parent powershell.exe tree, quarantine the ZIP it was extracted from. Vanilla Tempest hands off to Rhysida ransomware — speed matters. Hunt: Pivot on the user across the prior 4h for the originating ClickFix Edge "security update" lure URL; check other hosts that hit the same compromised WordPress sites (architecture/legal/construction-tech sectors per BlueVoyant report).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName =~ "node.exe"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\AppData\", @"\Temp\", @"\Downloads\", @"\Users\Public\", @"\ProgramData\")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| extend IsLegacyNode = (ProcessVersionInfoProductVersion startswith "7.10" or ProcessVersionInfoProductVersion startswith "7." or isempty(ProcessVersionInfoProductVersion))
| where IsLegacyNode
   or ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has "Node.js Foundation"
   or ProcessVersionInfoProductName has "Node.js"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, ProcessVersionInfoProductVersion, ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\node.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\AppData\\", "\\Temp\\", "\\Downloads\\", "\\Users\\Public\\", "\\ProgramData\\")
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Outdated Node.js Executed From User-Writable Path
id: 8a4f1d2c-3b5e-49a7-9d6b-2e8f4a1c7d35

description: Lorem Ipsum Loader bundles an outdated 2017 Node.js (v7.10.1) inside its ClickFix-delivered ZIP to execute the JavaScript dropper payload, evading EDR that allowlists modern signed node.exe. Flags any node.exe running from %TEMP%, %APPDATA%, %DOWNLOADS%, %PROGRAMDATA%, or %PUBLIC%.
references:

#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\node\.exe$/i
| ImageFileName=/\\(AppData|Temp|Downloads|Users\\Public|ProgramData)\\/i

ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime FROM datamodel=Endpoint.Processes WHERE Processes.process_name=node.exe AND (Processes.process_path="*\\AppData\\*" OR Processes.process_path="*\\Temp\\*" OR Processes.process_path="*\\Downloads\\*" OR Processes.process_path="*\\Users\\Public\\*" OR Processes.process_path="*\\ProgramData\\*") BY Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_path Processes.process Processes.process_hash Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`

DLL side-load of mscoree.dll or msvcp140.dll from non-System32 path (Lorem Ipsum) AIInstallation High
Lorem Ipsum Loader's batch-script persistence drops a malicious mscoree.dll or msvcp140.dll alongside a legitimate signed binary in a user-writable directory, then launches that binary so it loads the rogue DLL via search-order hijack. Detects image loads of these specific Windows runtime DLLs from anywhere other than the System32/SysWOW64/WinSxS/Program Files locations they legitimately live in. Rationale: Article explicitly names "mscoree.dll" and "msvcp140.dll" as the DLLs hijacked in the Lorem Ipsum side-load chain to decode the embedded loader. These two specific runtime DLLs are the highest-fidelity strings the article gives us — they should never legitimately load from %APPDATA%/%TEMP%/%PUBLIC%.
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Portable .NET app extracted to a user folder that ships a private mscoree shim (very rare in enterprise)
  • Indie game launcher bundling its own msvcp140.dll in a Public Documents games folder
  • Setup wizard temporarily extracting runtime DLLs to %TEMP% during MSI install
  • Legitimate vendor app installed under %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\<vendor>\ shipping msvcp140 redistributable
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("setup.exe", "installer.exe", "msiexec.exe", "vc_redist.x64.exe", "vcredist_x86.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "\\Microsoft\\EdgeUpdate\\"
Response runbook
Triage: Read the InitiatingProcess image — note the legit-looking signed binary it hijacks (often a small utility like 7zG.exe, Acrobat helpers, etc.). Hash both the host binary and the side-loaded DLL; submit DLL to sandbox to confirm Lorem Ipsum Loader payload (it should decode and reach out to a social-network profile URL). Contain: Isolate host, quarantine the entire folder containing both binaries, kill the host process. Check Run/RunOnce + Scheduled Tasks for the batch script that launches the side-load chain. Hunt: Look for the same SHA256 across the fleet (mass distribution), the originating ZIP in %DOWNLOADS%, and Edge browser history for the Edge "security update" lure URL that delivered it.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName in~ ("mscoree.dll", "msvcp140.dll")
| where FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\System32"
| where FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\SysWOW64"
| where FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\WinSxS"
| where FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\Microsoft.NET"
| where FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files"
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\AppData\", @"\Temp\", @"\Downloads\", @"\Users\Public\", @"\ProgramData\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where TargetFileName in~ ("mscoree.dll", "msvcp140.dll")
| where TargetFilePath !startswith @"C:\Windows\System32"
| where TargetFilePath !startswith @"C:\Windows\SysWOW64"
| where TargetFilePath !startswith @"C:\Windows\WinSxS"
| where TargetFilePath !startswith @"C:\Program Files"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\AppData\", @"\Temp\", @"\Downloads\", @"\Users\Public\", @"\ProgramData\")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Side-Load of mscoree.dll or msvcp140.dll From User-Writable Path
id: 9b5e6f3a-7c2d-4e1b-8a9f-3d4c6b8e2a47
status: experimental
description: Lorem Ipsum Loader's persistence chain plants a malicious mscoree.dll or msvcp140.dll next to a legitimate signed application in a user-writable directory and triggers a search-order hijack to decode the embedded loader payload. These specific runtime DLLs should only ever load from System32/SysWOW64/WinSxS/Program Files.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/clickfix-campaigns-expand-malware.html
author: SOC Detection Team
date: 2026/06/17
tags:
  - attack.defense_evasion
  - attack.persistence
  - attack.t1574.002
  - attack.t1036.005
logsource:
  category: image_load
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_dll:
    ImageLoaded|endswith:
      - '\mscoree.dll'
      - '\msvcp140.dll'
  selection_path:
    ImageLoaded|contains:
      - '\AppData\'
      - '\Temp\'
      - '\Downloads\'
      - '\Users\Public\'
      - '\ProgramData\'
  filter_legit:
    ImageLoaded|startswith:
      - 'C:\Windows\System32\'
      - 'C:\Windows\SysWOW64\'
      - 'C:\Windows\WinSxS\'
      - 'C:\Program Files\'
      - 'C:\Program Files (x86)\'
  condition: selection_dll and selection_path and not filter_legit
falsepositives:
  - Standalone .NET application installed into a user profile that ships its own mscoree shim (rare)
  - Game launchers / portable apps that bundle a private msvcp140.dll
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:7 (@ImageLoaded:*\\mscoree.dll OR @ImageLoaded:*\\MSCOREE.DLL OR @ImageLoaded:*\\msvcp140.dll OR @ImageLoaded:*\\MSVCP140.DLL) (@ImageLoaded:*\\AppData\\* OR @ImageLoaded:*\\Temp\\* OR @ImageLoaded:*\\Downloads\\* OR @ImageLoaded:*\\Users\\Public\\* OR @ImageLoaded:*\\ProgramData\\*) -@ImageLoaded:C\:\\Windows\\System32\\* -@ImageLoaded:C\:\\Windows\\SysWOW64\\* -@ImageLoaded:C\:\\Program\ Files*
#event_simpleName=ImageHash OR #event_simpleName=ClassifiedModuleLoad
| TargetFileName=/\\(mscoree|msvcp140)\.dll$/i
| regex("\\\\(AppData|Temp|Downloads|Users\\\\Public|ProgramData)\\\\", field=TargetFileName)
| NOT regex("^C:\\\\Windows\\\\(System32|SysWOW64|WinSxS|Microsoft\\.NET)\\\\", field=TargetFileName)
| NOT regex("^C:\\\\Program Files", field=TargetFileName)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName, SHA256HashData], function=count())
ENDPOINT
`sysmon` EventCode=7 ImageLoaded IN ("*\\mscoree.dll", "*\\msvcp140.dll") NOT ImageLoaded IN ("C:\\Windows\\System32\\*", "C:\\Windows\\SysWOW64\\*", "C:\\Windows\\WinSxS\\*", "C:\\Program Files\\*", "C:\\Program Files (x86)\\*") (Image="*\\AppData\\*" OR Image="*\\Temp\\*" OR Image="*\\Downloads\\*" OR Image="*\\Users\\Public\\*" OR Image="*\\ProgramData\\*") | stats min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Image) as Image values(ImageLoaded) as ImageLoaded values(User) as User count by Computer | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Potemkin host-marker file %LOCALAPPDATA%\hyper-v.ver creation AIInstallation High
Potemkin loader writes a per-victim UUID to %LOCALAPPDATA%\hyper-v.ver as its host identifier for C2 polling. The filename masquerades as a Hyper-V configuration artifact but Hyper-V never writes anything under %LOCALAPPDATA% — making this a near-zero-FP marker for Potemkin installation. Rationale: Article directly names "%LOCALAPPDATA%\hyper-v.ver" as the file Potemkin writes its UUID to for victim identification. Hyper-V config files live under %PROGRAMDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Hyper-V\ and the VM root paths — never %LOCALAPPDATA% — so this name+path combo is near-deterministic for Potemkin presence.
ATT&CKT1082 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • No legitimate scenario identified — flag every hit
  • Theoretical: a forensic analyst manually creating the file to reproduce IR scenarios
  • Theoretical: another malware family copy-catting Potemkin's marker filename
Response runbook
Triage: Note the InitiatingProcess — Potemkin's loader runs out of MSI/HTA → reflective load, so the writer is often rundll32.exe, regsvr32.exe, or a renamed binary in %APPDATA%. Read the file contents (it's the victim UUID, useful for cross-host correlation). Contain: Isolate immediately — Potemkin reflectively loads follow-on modules (RMMProject, EtherRAT) for credential theft. Kill all child processes of the writer. Hunt: Search %LOCALAPPDATA%\hyper-v.ver across the entire fleet for the same UUID file — same UUID across hosts means re-imaging from a poisoned baseline. Pivot on the UUID string in DNS query patterns (Potemkin DGA uses a 1,000-word dictionary so look for clusters of ~10 dictionary-word lookups from the same host).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName =~ "hyper-v.ver"
| where FolderPath has @"\AppData\Local\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName =~ "hyper-v.ver"
| where TargetFilePath has @"\AppData\Local\"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Potemkin Loader Host UUID Marker File
id: 4c8d9e7b-2a1f-4b6e-9d3c-5f7a8b1e3d49
status: experimental
description: Potemkin loader writes its per-victim UUID identifier to %LOCALAPPDATA%\hyper-v.ver for DGA-driven C2 polling. The filename impersonates a Hyper-V configuration file but Hyper-V never writes to %LOCALAPPDATA%, making this a high-fidelity infection marker.
references:
